news.title: US House Rejects Bid to Limit Supreme Court to Nine Justices
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The US House of Representatives has rejected a Republican-backed effort to permanently set the number of Supreme Court justices at nine, amid a broader political debate over the court’s conservative majority.According to Al Jazeera, the proposal failed to secure the two-thirds majority required for a constitutional amendment, with lawmakers voting 212 in favor and 206 against. The vote largely followed party lines, with North Carolina Democrat Don Davis the only Democrat to support the measure.What Happened in the House Vote?Republicans introduced a joint resolution that would have amended the US Constitution to permanently limit the Supreme Court to nine justices.The proposal fell well short of the two-thirds support required for constitutional amendments. By contrast, ordinary legislation generally requires only a simple majority in the House.The vote came a day after the House approved a resolution condemning socialism by 220-192, with eight Democrats joining Republicans.House Speaker Mike Johnson criticized Democrats who opposed both measures, arguing that supporting the Constitution and defending the Supreme Court should not be controversial.Republicans' efforts have been viewed largely as political messaging ahead of the November midterm elections, seeking to put Democrats on record over issues including socialism and possible expansion of the Supreme Court.Why Is the Supreme Court’s Size Being Debated?The debate stems partly from calls by some Democrats to expand the Supreme Court in response to its conservative majority.The idea, often called “court packing” by opponents, gained renewed attention after former President Donald Trump appointed three justices during his first term. The conservative-leaning court subsequently delivered several legal victories to Trump.In 2021, four Democratic lawmakers introduced legislation that would have expanded the Supreme Court to 13 justices. They argued that the move would restore balance to the court after what they described as Republican efforts to reshape the judiciary.More recently, Democratic Senator Jim Clyburn of South Carolina backed the idea of a 13-member court, while former Vice President Kamala Harris said Democrats should have a serious discussion about expanding the court.Republicans have strongly opposed such proposals, arguing that changes could undermine the independence of the federal judiciary.Does the US Constitution Set the Number of Justices?No. Although the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court, it does not specify how many justices must sit on the court.Congress has therefore determined the court’s size through legislation over the country's history.The Judiciary Act of 1789 initially established a six-member Supreme Court, consisting of a chief justice and five associate justices. The number changed several times during the 19th century before Congress set the current number of nine justices in 1869.That history means the number of Supreme Court seats is not constitutionally fixed and can be changed by Congress without amending the Constitution.Has the Supreme Court Been Expanded Before?Yes. The size of the Supreme Court has changed several times since its creation.The most famous modern attempt to expand the court came from President Franklin D. Roosevelt after he won reelection in 1936.Roosevelt proposed adding justices based on the age of sitting members, potentially allowing up to six additional justices. The plan became known as the “court-packing” proposal and faced strong opposition.More recently, groups including the Brennan Center for Justice have advocated structural reforms such as term limits and ethics rules, while some Democratic lawmakers have continued to support expanding the court.The issue has now returned to the political spotlight as the United States approaches another closely watched midterm election.Read: US Supreme Court Allows Trump Ballroom Project to ProceedClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: US House rejects a Republican-backed bid to limit the Supreme Court to nine justices, amid a wider fight over the court's conservative majority.

news.title: Donald Trump Beats Zohran Mamdani on Net Favorability: New Poll
news.text: President Donald Trump has a more favorable net favorability rating than New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to a new Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, though both men are underwater among voters as two of the most recognizable faces of their respective parties. Trump has a net favorability rating of -8 percent, with 42 percent of registered voters viewing him favorably and 50 percent unfavorably, according to the poll. Mamdani, meanwhile, has a net favorability rating of -14 percent, with 25 percent viewing him favorably and 39 percent unfavorably. The poll surveyed 2,100 registered voters from August 28-30, 2026, and has a margin of error of 2.1 percent. The numbers are notable because Trump and Mamdani have become defining figures for the Republican and Democratic parties, respectively. Trump has reshaped the GOP around his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, while Mamdani's rapid rise has made him one of the most prominent figures associated with the Democratic Party's progressive wing. Newsweek reached out to the White House and Mamdani's office via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll found that 51 percent of voters believe the Democratic Party is being taken over by the far left, while 45 percent believe the Republican Party is being taken over by the far right. Mamdani's rise has nevertheless represented a significant shift within the Democratic Party. His progressive agenda and upset victory over establishment Democrat Andrew Cuomo in New York's mayoral primary have made him a national political figure, while also fueling debate over whether Democrats should embrace his brand of politics or distance themselves from it. Trump faces a similar dynamic on the Republican side, where his continued dominance has made it somewhat difficult for the party to separate itself from his agenda and political style. The result is a striking political paradox: Trump and Mamdani may be among the clearest faces of America's increasingly polarized parties, but neither is viewed favorably by a majority of Americans, according to the new poll. As both parties look toward the 2026 midterm elections, the question may be whether voters want more of the political movements these two men represent—or something different altogether. Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Wednesday, "This probably reflects the fact that President Trump and the Republicans have made socialism and Mamdani a central target of their negative messaging in recent weeks. It’s having an effect, apparently." "Mamdani is also actually making changes, and has had some glitches with staff, etc., and as those mount that will take some shine off of the 'young phenom' effect he’s been enjoying. But that doesn’t explain the national numbers, because most Americans don’t follow day-to-day policy and politics in NYC," he added. When asked if Americans view both Trump and Mamdani as leaders of their party, Reeher later said, "The president is always the de facto leader of his party. Trump is no different, but there are divisions within the ranks, on both the Iran war and the tariffs. I don’t see Mamdani as the recognized 'leader' of the Democratic Party, and doubt he ever will be. He’s one of the principal leaders of the Left wing of the party, that’s for sure. I don’t think the party has a particular leader at the moment, to be honest." Florida Atlantic University politics professor Craig Agranoff also told Newsweek on Wednesday when asked about the net favorability numbers, "A month-to-month flip like this is not shocking." "National favorability for both men moves with the news cycle, and Mamdani is still building name recognition outside New York. Trump remains far better known, so his numbers are more settled even when they sit underwater. That does not make either man the uncontested leader of his party. Trump is still the central figure on the Republican side because he occupies the White House and defines the coalition," Agranoff added. "Mamdani is a rising face of the Democratic left, but the party still has multiple power centers and he does not yet speak for the whole national brand. Favorability gaps this size tell you more about visibility and polarization than about who actually runs either party." Meanwhile, the Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll shows only two U.S. political figures with positive net favorability: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump's net favorability in the poll is worse than former Vice President Kamala Harris, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and House Speaker Mike Johnson. The poll shows Trump's net favorability is better than California Governor Gavin Newsom, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Tucker Carlson and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan. What Polls Show Other polling, however, has shown that Mamdani's favorability has been positive as he has settled into office. An early-August Siena College poll found 47 percent of New York likely voters viewed him favorably, compared with 44 percent who viewed him unfavorably, while other polling around his first 100 days in office showed 48 percent of New Yorkers approving of his performance and 30 percent disapproving. July's Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed Trump's net favorability at -13 percent, with 40 percent net favorability compared to 53 percent net unfavorability. The poll showed Mamdani with a net favorability of -7 percent, with 27 percent net favorability and 35 percent net unfavorability. That poll surveyed 1,776 registered voters from July 11-12, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.3 percent. A Siena University poll taken in June showed Trump's favorability at 32 percent, compared with 63 percent unfavorable. The survey showed that Mamdani's favorability was positive, at 45 percent, compared to 34 percent unfavorable. The poll surveyed 1,120 New York State registered voters from June 17-23, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.6 percent. A May Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed that Trump's net favorability was -6 percent, with a 43 percent net favorable rating compared to 50 percent net unfavorability. Mamdani's net favorability rating was 23 percent compared to a net 33 percent unfavorable rating. Mamdani's overall net favorability in the poll was -10 percent. The poll surveyed 1,725 registered voters from May 29-31, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.4 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Trump has reshaped the GOP around MAGA, while Mamdani has emerged as a leading figure of the Democratic Party's progressive wing.

news.title: 1 in 6 Trump voters would change their 2024 vote, poll finds
news.text:
Nearly two years after Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris to win back the White House, some of the voters who helped put him there are having second thoughts.

A new University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov poll found that 16% of Trump voters say they would change their 2024 vote if given the chance. An even larger share, 21%, said they now have second thoughts about supporting the president.

The findings come as Trump's approval ratings remain underwater in multiple national surveys and amid concerns over the economy, rising prices and the ongoing war in Iran.

Why it matters

The poll, released Aug. 31, found that 57% of respondents believe Trump has performed worse than they expected since returning to office in 2025. The survey also showed Trump's approval rating at 32%, down one percentage point from the university's previous poll in April.

The results were released the same day a Reuters/Ipsos survey found Trump's job approval rating holding at 33% for a third straight week, marking his lowest rating in that poll since returning to office.

The University of Massachusetts Amherst/YouGov survey polled 1,000 respondents from Aug. 21-26 and has a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points.

Iran, inflation weigh on voters

The survey suggests voters remain frustrated by several issues facing the administration, particularly the ongoing conflict with Iran and rising consumer costs.

Only 26% of respondents said they approve of the war in Iran, and roughly 1 in 4 said they believe the United States is winning the conflict.

"With no end in sight to the ongoing war in Iran, the continued rise in the price of gas, groceries, utilities, and housing, an escalating trade war with Canada, and the likelihood of higher interest rates, it comes as no surprise that Trump's approval rating remains at a paltry 32%," Tatishe Nteta, director of the UMass Amherst Poll, said in a news release.

According to AAA, the national average price for a gallon of gas stood at $4.12 on Sept. 2, up 3 cents from a month earlier and nearly $1 higher than a year ago.

What do polling averages show?

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Sept. 1): 39.9% approve, 56.6% disapproveNew York Times (Sept. 1): 38% approve, 58% disapproveSilver Bulletin (Sept. 1): 38.2% approve, 58% disapprove

USA TODAY’s Kinsey Crowley contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: Two Dems clashed on trans athletes. What does Markey's primary win reveal?
news.text:
Rep. Seth Moulton was among the first Democrats after the 2024 elections to publicly question his party’s support for the inclusion of transgender athletes in sports. 

That decision, and the backlash that followed, likely contributed to his loss in Massachusetts' Sept. 1 primary against 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey.

Two years after Republicans made transgender rights a central focus of their 2024 election attack ads, Democrats are still working through how to message on an issue that is deeply important to their base, but polls poorly with much of the electorate.

Moulton, 47, centered his campaign on generational change and the need for new blood in Congress. But Markey was able to easily fend off the challenge by emphasizing his progressive platform, including support for transgender rights.

The senator contrasted his message with remarks Moulton made after Democrats lost up and down the ticket in the 2024 election, when Moulton told The New York Times that he didn’t want his two young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete,” a comment Moulton said he was supposed to be “afraid to say" as a Democrat.

While Markey's progressive politics helped him in Massachusetts, Democrats competing outside the bluest states in the country are already facing a new wave of attacks ads on transgender rights, specifically regarding girls' and women's sports.

“There's no doubt in my mind that this is going to come up in every single race at every single level, and Democrats have to be prepared to respond,” said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at Third Way, a center-left think tank. “What we've seen is if people think that what the Republicans are saying is true, they think that Democrats are extreme.”

Markey took on Moulton's comments on trans athletes

During the 2024 presidential election cycle, Donald Trump’s campaign spent millions of dollars on ads attacking then-Vice President Kamala Harris for her stances on transgender rights, arguing that Harris was “for they/them” and Trump was “for you.” The president and his campaign said Harris also supported taxpayer funded gender affirming care for detainees, likely referring to a 2019 ACLU questionnaire where Harris agreed to ensure medical care for transgender and nonbinary people who "rely on the state - including those in prison and immigration detention."

After the election, Moulton and a handful of other prominent Democrats sought to push their party to have a debate over its stance on transgender athletes in girls sports. 

Markey made Moulton’s comments a focal point of his primary campaign. After the congressman announced his challenge, Markey appeared at a No Kings rally draped in a transgender pride flag. 

Moulton sought to pivot left on the issue during the campaign.

He signed onto the Transgender Bill of Rights in the House. At a debate last month, the congressman apologized for his comments to The New York Times and said transgender athletes “should” be able to participate in sports leagues that match their gender identity, with some safety qualifications. 

Markey said Moulton “threw those kids under the political bus after the election” and turned them into “political fodder.” 

Transgender athletes a topic in competitive states

Democrats are still weighing how to discuss transgender athlete participation in battleground races, where public opinion is likely less favorable. A 2025 Gallup poll found that 69% of Americans oppose allowing transgender athletes to play on the teams that match their gender identity, up from 62% in 2021. 

“The Democrats are never going to win on that issue,” said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. “This is not a close call.”

Rob Sand, Iowa's Democratic nominee for governor, has been opposed to allowing transgender girls to participate in girls sports leagues throughout his campaign. Trump won Iowa in all three of his presidential campaigns, but the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the seat a Lean Democratic race. 

"I have said, consistently, I think that fairness rules the day in girls' sports,” Sand told Politico last month. "I just think girls' sports are for girls, and boys' sports are for boys. And I think that that's fair and reasonable."

Democrat Amy Acton, a former public health official running for governor in Ohio, said in June she doesn’t support “boys playing in girls sports” and would enforce the state’s ban on school age transgender athletes participating in sports. Equality Ohio, an LGBTQ rights group, changed her rating from A to pending as a result of her comments. 

Democrats have been most effective, Erickson said, when they say they want sports to be fair and safe, and support allowing sports associations to set the rules. Candidates have also had success noting that bans on transgender athletes can lead to invasive gender checks on children, she said.

Erickson and other Democratic strategists pointed to Abigail Spanberger’s successful 2025 Virginia gubernatorial campaign, in which she quickly responded to attacks on transgender rights from her Republican opponent and called on politicians to “trust parents and local communities” to set rules on transgender athlete participation. 

Tyler Hack, the executive director of the Christopher Street Project, a transgender rights group, said that in a blue state like Massachusetts allyship looks like Markey’s “unapologetic defense” of transgender rights.

But the organization is also working with candidates in tough races on how to talk about transgender athletes and other issues in ways that resonate with voters in their districts. 

“If candidates want to talk about this issue through a lens of local participation, and if that works for them, I have no problem with that. The problem is when you have candidates call transgender girls boys,” Hack said. “That is a hard line for our party, and last night should show that that's not where voters are.”

news.title: Kamala Harris Suffers Embarrassing 'Jeopardy!' Snub — as All 3 Contestants Are Left Stumped by Question About Ex-Veep
news.text:
Jeopardy! contestants unintentionally dealt former Vice President Kamala Harris an embarrassing blow, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

When asked to identify the name of her memoir, all three contestants on the iconic game show were left without words.'Jeopardy!' Contestants Left Stumped Over Kamala Harris ClueThe trivia experts were given the prompt, "The title of this 2025 memoir by Kamala Harris refers to how long she had to launch and run her 2024 presidential campaign," by host Ken Jennings.

The tell-all book title, though, was not identified by any of the competitors, resulting in the show's signature beeping sound. The answer would be, "What is 107 Days?"

"She had 107 days," Jennings told the contestants.Kamala Harris' Memoir Describes Her Presidential CampaignHarris' memoir described her much-shortened bid for the presidency in 2024. Harris was former President Joe Biden's running mate as he attempted to secure the White House for a second term. However, after public outcry due to concerns over his health, he stepped aside, allowing Harris to take over.

Initial criticism mounted over the fact that Harris was not technically the Democratic Party nominee. However, the party was forced to rally behind her in the unprecedented move as they faced Donald Trump.

Harris attempted to overcome dissent among her own party and make up for lost time. She was unsuccessful. 

After losing the election, she stepped out of the public eye as she thought up her next move. During that time, the 61-year-old drafted a memoir to reflect on the struggles she faced.Kamala Harris' Memoir Receives Positive ReviewsIn announcing her book, Harris said in a video, "Just over a year ago, I launched my campaign for President of the United States. 107 days traveling the country, fighting for our future – the shortest presidential campaign in modern history. Since leaving office, I’ve spent a lot of time reflecting on those days, and with candor and reflection, I’ve written a behind-the-scenes account of that journey. I believe there’s value in sharing what I saw, what I learned, and what it will take to move forward."

While Jeopardy! contestants weren't quick to recall its release, the book did garner decent reviews.

One person wrote, "I had mixed feelings about reading this book. Not because I have mixed feelings about Harris, but because the gut-punch from her loss still stings to this day, especially when the news is a constant removal of a barely formed and tentative scab. I wasn't sure I could handle reliving the trauma of the last election and the outcome."

Another noted,, "Kamala Harris tells us that when we fight, we win, but sometimes, the fight takes a while. We must play the long game."Presidential Bid for Kamala Harris UnknownAs for Harris' political future, it's uncertain. She has not yet announced an official bid, and Democrats are split on whether they'd like to see her run again.

On April 10, 2026, during an on-stage interview with Al Sharpton, she was asked if she plans to run again. 

"I might. I am thinking about it," she responded at the time.
news.summary: 'Jeopardy!' contestants were at a loss when they were asked to reflect on the former vice president's memoir release.

news.title: Voters Say They Want Younger Politicians. So Why Do They Keep Voting for Old Ones?
news.text:
Here’s a paradox for you: In overwhelming numbers, voters keep telling pollsters that they want upper age limits and term limits for members of Congress. At the same time, they keep voting to reelect long-serving lawmakers who are in their 70s and 80s.

Massachusetts offers the latest evidence. Older incumbents of all ideological stripes swept the state’s Democratic primaries last night. In the race for U.S. Senate, two-term Sen. Ed Markey, an 80-year-old progressive, easily dispatched the more moderate Rep. Seth Moulton, 47. Elsewhere, Reps. Richard Neal and Stephen Lynch, who are both in their 70s and have collectively been in office for more than six decades, fended off younger and leftier challengers.

So what’s really going on? Here are a few theories.

Ideology over age

As the saying goes, age is but a number. Yet voters keep telling us it’s actually a lot more than that. At first glance, Markey’s win would seem to break a recent streak of older incumbents falling to more youthful candidates. So far this year, the losers include Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York (71), Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan (71), and Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado (69). But Markey’s victory also fits a different pattern: In all three of those earlier races, the elder lawmaker lost to a more outspokenly progressive rival. And for Massachusetts Democrats contemplating who they wanted as their next senator, ideology was clearly more important than age.

When Moulton launched his campaign, he downplayed any real policy differences with Markey. “Sen. Markey is a good man, but it’s time for a new generation of leadership,” he said in his announcement video. Markey, though, hammered the issues where they did diverge—including the debate over transgender rights. After Kamala Harris lost in 2024, a defeat some Democrats attributed in part to a viral pro-Trump ad that argued “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you,” Moulton expressed opposition to trans athletes playing in women’s sports. “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete,” he told the New York Times.

Moulton later retreated from those remarks (“I’m sorry if my comments hurt you,” he told the trans community last month), but Markey sought to make them stick. “Trans rights are human rights,” the senator said recently. In a preelection poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, two-thirds of likely Democratic primary voters said they were less likely to support a candidate who had opposed trans rights, and about the same share said they trusted Markey to better represent them on the issues they cared about. So going forward, it’s probably better to think of age as a factor, but rarely the factor, in how voters approach candidates.

The power of incumbency

Moulton’s drubbing has some progressives crowing that new ideas, not just fresh faces, are what Democrats need to compete. How, then, to explain the survival of Neal and Lynch, two longtime members of Congress who put down progressive challenges from first-time candidates last night?

One answer is straightforward: Politicians who seek reelection almost always win. Nationwide, 95 percent of all incumbents reclaimed their seats in 2024. Journalists have showered ink on the anti-establishment fervor that’s supposedly sweeping the Democratic Party, buoyed by voters furious over its longtime leaders’ failure to prevent Donald Trump’s return. But even in that treacherous environment, only seven sitting House Democrats have lost renomination so far this year, a tiny fraction of those running for reelection. Lynch and Neal both won relatively narrowly, which may suggest some frustration with their long tenures or more centrist records (or both). But there’s clearly a risk of overstating Democrats’ unhappiness with their party’s old guard—and of mapping that anger too neatly onto ideology.

Health, not age

Polling is an imperfect instrument, and asking voters whether they favor a given candidate or policy doesn’t always tell you why they feel the way they do. So another possible explanation for the apparent paradox over older politicians is that age, at least by itself, isn’t really what voters are worried about. The better term for what’s on their minds may instead be health, both cognitive and physical.

The clearest example is what happened last month, when Rep. John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat who has represented Connecticut since 1999, lost his primary to a younger challenger. But Larson wasn’t just old and established. He had a complex partial seizure while delivering an on-camera speech on the House floor last year, stopping midsentence before continuing to speak in a slow and halting voice for more than 30 seconds. Larson’s office later attributed the seizure to a congenital heart issue, adding that he’d been prescribed medication to help. But it’s not all that shocking that voters declined to return him to Congress, opting instead for a 47-year-old former mayor who campaigned on generational change.

The health-over-age dynamic may also explain Markey’s resilience. As even some of Moulton’s supporters acknowledged, the 80-year-old senator still looks spry and sounds with it. (After a recent rally, Markey’s campaign blasted out video of the senator shooting hoops.) Markey would be 86 at the end of his next term, the same age Joe Biden would’ve been had he won and finished a second term, but voters evidently saw them differently. In a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll last month, only a third of Massachusetts primary voters said Markey’s age made them less inclined to support him. When Biden launched his reelection bid, on the other hand, even most Democrats told pollsters that he was too old for another term. They may have been alarmed less by the year on Biden’s birth certificate and more by his apparent physical frailty, softening voice, and questions about his mental acuity.

OK, time to switch gears. For your evening enjoyment, why not:

Take a break with this movie review: We regret to inform you that Raygun is back. The Aussie breakdancer who went viral in 2024 for her cringingly bad performance at the Summer Olympics in Paris is the subject of an infuriating new Netflix documentary about the whole ordeal. Slate culture writer Nadira Goffe watched it so you don’t have to.

Soothe your inner child with some nostalgic tunes: When Rebecca Knight became a parent, she vowed that her kids wouldn’t listen to Raffi. But she quickly realized the error of her ways, thanks to a Laura Marling album of Raffi covers. (If you want to learn more about Raffi’s singular status in the world of kids’ music, listen to this 2023 episode of Working in which the artist breaks down his creative decisions.)

Get in the back-to-school spirit: It can be hard to adjust to the end of summer vacation. But there is one small part of the new school year that is guaranteed to enthrall students, parents, and teachers alike. Slate staff writer Heather Schwedel investigates why lamination—a hallmark of an organized classroom—has such a hold on both kids and grown-ups.

Give your brain a workout: Who is “Wonder Woman’s godly enemy” (four letters)? Which city “has a Jewish population that is neither Sephardic or Ashkenazi” (four letters)? Test your wordplay skills with today’s crossword.

Alas, writing this newsletter has exhausted my wordplay skills, so I’m off to walk the dog instead. Enjoy the rest of your night!
news.summary: The gerontocracy strikes back.
news.author: Ian Prasad Philbrick

news.title: Republicans fail to ease one of Trump's greatest fears as Supreme Court measure collapses
news.text: House Democrats are nuking Republicans' effort to assuage one of President Donald Trump's biggest concerns about the future of the federal government. A vote on a constitutional amendment to cap the number of Supreme Court justices failed on Wednesday afternoon after the vast majority of Democrats voted against it. Trump has warned for months that he believes Democrats would seek to expand the Supreme Court if they took back control of Congress, something affirmed by top progressives, including former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. House GOP leaders sought to head that off with a proposed amendment led by Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., that would mandate that just nine justices can sit on the high court. KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., opted to fast-track the legislation past multiple procedural hurdles in exchange for raising the threshold for passage from a simple majority to two-thirds, a maneuver known as "suspending the rules." But it failed to clinch that number, even though the majority of House lawmakers supported the amendment. The U.S. Constitution allows Congress to set the number of seats on the Supreme Court bench, which is currently occupied by eight justices and one chief justice. However, the Constitution itself does not dictate how many justices can exist. Republicans argued that changing that could make it much harder for a Democrat-led government to pack the court in the future to stack judicial odds in its favor. CARVILLE TELLS DEMS TO QUIETLY PREPARE POWER GRAB WITH DC, PUERTO RICO STATEHOOD AND SUPREME COURT PACKING "Here's the question every American should ask: If a sitting majority can change the size of the Supreme Court the moment it dislikes rulings, what happens to the next time the other side is in power?" Biggs asked Wednesday. "Once you go down that road, the court stops being an independent check on government power. It becomes another political institution controlled by whoever happens to hold the majority." Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., among the progressives calling to increase the number of justices to 13, argued that Congress has changed the number of Supreme Court justices multiple times throughout history and dismissed the current tally as arbitrary. "MAGA's proposal is to strip Congress of all authority in the matter, to freeze it and cement it permanently in the constitutional architecture for all time with the suddenly magic number nine," Raskin said. "It's another partisan power grab by MAGA, our colleagues, who fear for the results of the November election as their policies have brought us nothing but war, inflation, corruption, lawlessness and a $40 trillion debt — one quarter of it's supplied by this presidential administration. So, the MAGA party wants to cement into place a profoundly partisan and lopsided ... court that was gerrymandered and engineered by Mitch McConnell." HARRIS LABELED 'INSTITUTIONAL ARSONIST' FOR PLAN TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM SCOTUS AND ELECTORAL COLLEGE He was referring to former Senate GOP Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and his critical role in helping secure the current conservative majority on the high court. Progressives have argued that expanding the court to 13 would mean there is one justice for every federal circuit court. Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., attacked the left's push as an effort to seize political power. "For decades, we have heard calls from those unhappy with the ideological balance of the Supreme Court to pack the court. The alarming rise of such calls should worry all of us, because their objective is not to uphold ethical principles or even to protect individual rights, but rather to consolidate power and intimidate the court," Harris said. Later, Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., said locking the number at nine would only extend the current conservative majority's power. news.summary: House Democrats blocked a constitutional amendment to cap Supreme Court justices at nine after President Donald Trump warned of future court packing.

news.title: Book reviews: ‘The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy’ and ‘The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence’
news.text:
‘The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy’ by Gil Durán

“Picture this: A loosely organized cabal of obscenely wealthy tech moguls aim to overthrow democracy and replace it with a corporatist dictatorship,” said Kevin Truong in . The premise, undoubtedly, “would make for a good political thriller.” In Gil Durán’s new nonfiction hit, it makes for more unsettling reading. Durán, a journalist who’s also been a spokesman for Jerry Brown and Kamala Harris, argues that tech entrepreneur Peter Thiel, the main patron of JD Vance’s career, sits at the center of an active and powerful circle of tech evangelists who believe democracy is obsolete, technology will create a utopian future, and their cohort is an elite that should decide how the future unfolds. The claim would sound like mere conspiracy theory, said Tonya Mosley in , except that the players Durán identifies “have been stating their beliefs and aspirations out loud for years.”“You could not ask for a more hair-raising compendium of the insane things that Silicon Valley moguls have advocated for,” said Laura Miller in . Thiel, a co-founder of PayPal and Palantir, has touted as formative to his beliefs a 1997 book, The Sovereign Individual, that arguably predicted the rise of cryptocurrency and AI while also forecasting the collapse of nation-states and emergence of individuals smart and powerful enough to pursue their ambitions without constraint. Thiel can count Elon Musk and fellow venture capitalist Marc Andreessen among his allies, and all appear to have been influenced by alt-right blogger Curtis Yarvin, who advocates putting the U.S. under the rule of a CEO-style monarch and has talked about the need to develop “a humane alternative to genocide” to address Earth’s supposed excess of unproductive individuals. While Durán “gives perhaps too much credence to the viability of Silicon Valley’s most authoritarian dreams,” his book is a “much-needed” wake-up call, warning us that today’s tech giants should be feared, not blindly worshipped.Durán claims that tech moguls view the Trump regime as a vehicle for the expansion of their power, and “few could dispute this,” said Steve Rose in . Remember the many tech titans standing behind him at his 2025 inauguration? Or how they helped the Trump family make billions off cryptocurrency? The payoffs have come in government contracts such as Palantir’s estimated $13.7 billion annual haul as well as in the wrecking ball taken to government oversight. Trump has even backed such nutty ideas as building 10 “Freedom Cities” that would be exempt from many existing regulations. Thiel and his allies haven’t fully triumphed yet, though, as indicated by the recent surge in public opposition to data centers. With any luck, “this could be a radicalizing moment.”

‘The Ego Trip: Psychedelic Toads, a Trail of Deaths, and the Guru Who Peddled Transcendence’ by Kimon de Greef

“Readers who are unaware that the secretions from some toads may serve as portals to the divine are in for some significant revelations,” said Dave Shiflett in . Kimon de Greef’s engaging new book takes as a given that the Sonoran Desert toad produces 5-MeO-DMT, a powerful natural psychedelic. But de Greef is also interested in the subculture that’s arisen around “the God molecule,” as advocates call it. Toad facilitators now regularly milk the toad’s glands and dry the extract so it can be smoked, generating potent trips that are said to collapse the ego. Toad smoking can cause instant psychosis, but fans of the practice include Mike Tyson and Hunter Biden, and “de Greef describes the effects of 5-MeO-DMT in such glowing terms that a foot-washing Baptist might be tempted to give it a shot.”

“For an experience this intense, a wise guide is key—or so you’d think,” said Susannah Cahalan in . The antihero of de Greef’s story is Octavio Rettig Hinojosa, a Mexican doctor turned psychedelic celebrity who, since 2006, has championed toad smoking, claiming the practice helped him kick crack. Since achieving widespread fame in 2013, Rettig has overseen gatherings that have introduced thousands of novices to toad smoking. “If you’re familiar with the guru playbook, you know where this is going.” Rettig’s recklessness has led to suffering. At one point, he was charged in the death of a woman who stopped breathing during one of his ceremonies.

“As de Greef is keen to stress, the problem is not just one eccentric doctor,” said Lilia Marie Ellis in the . Though 5-MeO-DMT is illegal in the U.S., pharmaceutical companies are displaying similar heedlessness as they race to monetize synthesized versions, which have shown promise in the treatment of addiction and post-traumatic stress disorder. De Greef’s book “stalls slightly” when it turns away from Rettig, “whose energy jumps off the page.” Still, The Ego Trip “succeeds in illustrating that commercialized psychedelics are not the miracle drug many hoped for.”
news.summary: A look at how tech evangelists are trying to stifle democracy and the rise and fall of a toad smoking enthusiast
news.author: The Week US

news.title: The 8 biggest issues that will determine the midterms
news.text:
Democrats are broadcasting cautious optimism as they head into the final stretch ahead of the 2026 midterms. As the party out of power, they are traditionally favored to make major gains when polls close in November. Republicans are meanwhile scrambling to defend their congressional majorities in the face of historic headwinds and flagging popularity.

While each of the hundreds of midterm races is a unique contest shaped by the variety of candidates and communities therein, there are certain issues that have emerged as electoral inflection points nationwide. Rising costs of living, increasingly heavy-handed immigration actions and a raging debate over transgender inclusion are just some of the factors that will likely determine who controls Congress — and to what end — come January.

Cost of living

Democrats have “gained a significant edge” over Republicans on “voter perceptions” about which party is better suited to address the rising cost of living, said Reuters. For the past year, voters have “signaled the cost of living will be the most important factor” in their midterm choices. Trump, however, has “mostly dismissed concerns about the high cost of living during his second term,” said Roll Call, “including the price of gasoline” since “joining Israel in an armed conflict with Iran.” Although it was the “financial frustration of a pandemic-weary electorate” that helped push Trump back into office in 2024, the president’s “actions in office have complicated, if not undermined” many of his promises for financial relief, said The New York Times.

Data centers

The ongoing debate over data centers is “suddenly at the epicenter of the midterm elections,” said The New York Times. Politicians of all stripes are “racing to tap into the backlash — or inoculate themselves” — from what has become an “unusually fast-moving force that is already reshaping races for the House, the Senate and governor’s mansions.” $31 million has been spent this year on data center-focused political ads, “spiking” in July when “more than 8% of all campaign spending on broadcast TV went to data center or AI-related spots,” said CNN. This is “up significantly” from “less than 1% of ads last year.”

Because of the “huge tracts of land” needed to accommodate mammoth computing warehouses, tech companies have “been exploring deeper into rural America,” said PBS News. That has, in turn, “united conservative ranching and farming communities” with “left-leaning environmental advocacy groups” over their “combined concern.”

Donald Trump

Despite being the “most potent force in Republican primary elections,” Trump himself “may soon be something entirely different for Republican candidates,” said The New York Times: a “liability.” Trump’s approval is “well underwater” thanks to “rising prices and an unpopular war.” Accordingly, Democrats have moved to target battleground Republican candidates by “tying them” to the president in the hopes they can “ride voter anger with his administration to congressional majorities.”

Trump may be “on a mission to burnish his legacy,” said The Wall Street Journal, but some GOP insiders “privately worry that Trump’s focus on himself is backfiring with voters.” For his part, the president has reportedly decided to “lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself,” said The Atlantic. To that end, Trump has commissioned a “series of television advertisements about his own record” that will “serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests.”

Republicans may have “hammered Democrats on gas prices” during the 2024 national elections, said Politico. But with prices “soaring” again amid ongoing hostilities with Iran, “this time, the roles are reversed.” This year already, approximately “two-thirds of ads mentioning gas prices” are from Democratic candidates and groups.

Rising gas prices are “becoming a major concern” for voters and “GOP lawmakers trying to hold onto their seats” alike, said MS NOW. Historical electoral analysis holds that incumbents “tend to pay a more significant electoral price” in midterm races “when costs at the pump are higher.” In March, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee purchased a suite of social media ads about rising fuel costs that targeted “about four dozen battleground districts” the party “believes can be flipped,” said USA Today.

Immigration

Republican lawmakers and candidates are hoping to “reverse the damage” that Trump’s deportations and immigration policies have done to voters, said Politico. Although immigration “was a reliable winner for Republicans” in elections past, the party is now “struggling not only to convince persuadable voters” but also to “hold together their own coalition as it splinters over deportations.”

With Immigration and Customs Enforcement “revving up its operations across the country,” the White House is making a move “fraught with political risk as the midterm elections draw closer,” said NBC News. “Moderate and progressive Democrats alike,” meanwhile, have “figured out how to talk about the border,” said Politico. But “with less than three months until Election Day,” they “still aren’t on the same page” when it comes to dealing with ICE.

“Some high-profile” Democratic candidates have campaigned by pushing ICE “reforms,” while others are “calling to dissolve the agency altogether,” said Politico. Although “many in the party see an opening” given how unpopular Trump’s anti-immigration policies have been overall, some Democrats “worry that going too far on ICE could again kneecap their electoral chances in key battlegrounds.”

Six months after President Trump declared war on Iran, the conflict between Washington and Tehran has “reshaped the rapidly approaching midterm election,” said The Associated Press. Not only have the months of violence undermined Trump’s campaign pledge to “steer clear of foreign conflicts,” the war is “challenging Republicans who would rather focus on their tax cuts” to defend their “narrow majorities in Congress.”

Republicans have urged the White House to “wrap up the conflict,” said The Atlantic, in the hopes of reducing the war’s “drag on the nation’s economy — and their reelection chances.” Although “poll after poll” has shown how unpopular the war is domestically, said CNN, Republicans remain “reluctant to publicly break with a president” who remains “popular inside their party.”

“Growing schisms” among Democrats over Israel have become a “contentious issue for the party,” said NPR, “particularly as it heads into the midterm election.” While some party insiders claim that the “divide” among lawmakers is “limited to military aid,” others say the “biggest gap” is “between the party’s elected officials and voters” who have “moved against Israel faster than their representatives” in the wake of Israeli military action in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The pivot on historical support for Israel has been “clearest on the Democratic left,” where candidates frame the powerful Israel lobbying group AIPAC as “emblematic of big-money interests overwhelming ordinary voters,” said France 24. But criticism has “spread to the populist right” as well. Some “America First” conservatives have “attacked Washington’s support for Israel and blamed pro-Israel lobbying for drawing the United States deeper into foreign conflicts.” Approaching the midterms, a “once-prized endorsement” from groups supporting Israel “can now, in some races, be something candidates would rather their opponents talked less about.”

Transgender rights

“Across the country,” Republican-run ads attacking Democrats over “transgender athletes’ sports participation and gender-affirming medical care for minors” have “become commonplace,” said PBS News. The nationwide push is part of an “effort to tap into a strategy that was successful for President Trump in 2024,” where he framed former Vice President Kamala Harris’ openness to transgender rights as being “outside the cultural mainstream.”

For Democrats, determining how candidates “should — or should not — respond to anti-trans attacks” has “since taken up a lot of oxygen in Washington as party strategists debate the best course forward,” said The 19th. Some Democrats are confident that anti-trans ads will “backfire on Republicans as Americans increasingly embrace transgender rights,” said The Washington Times, in much the same way the party “brought voters to their side on gay marriage.”
news.summary: Everything from gas prices to international relations will be on the ballot in November
news.author: Rafi Schwartz

news.title: Meet The Republicans Facing The Toughest Fights This November — And How They Plan To Keep Their Seats
news.text:
Midterm elections have historically favored the party out of power, putting Republicans on the defensive as they fight to maintain their majorities in Congress. With control of the House hinging on just a handful of competitive races, vulnerable Republicans are searching for different ways to survive a difficult political environment.

President Donald Trump’s approval is underwater, the war in Iran is weighing on voters, and affordability has emerged as the defining issue heading into November. These lawmakers are navigating some of the toughest races this November, and their campaigns have attracted the interest of National Democrats looking to retake the lower chamber on Election Day. 

New York Republican Mike Lawler was first elected to Congress in 2022 and has carved out a prominent political profile as a bipartisan dealmaker while maintaining a close relationship with President Donald Trump. Lawler faced a tough reelection in 2024; he was one of only three republicans to win a House district carried by then-Vice President Kamala Harris. This year, Lawler is up for another tough fight. He is facing veteran U.S. Army officer and former national security official Cait Conely. 

Conely calls herself a “proud fourth-generation Hudson Valley native from working-class roots who understands the values of hard work and public service.” (RELATED: Republicans Hope Trump’s Unprecedented Convention Can Rewrite Midterm History)

She’s attacked Lawler over his perceived closeness to the President, saying he will “do whatever Trump says.”

Lawler has walked a fine line during his congressional tenure, working to maintain a close relationship with the White House while still breaking with Republican House Leadership and the White House, most notably on the State and Local Tax (SALT) Deduction cap. SALT was widely seen as a top legislative priority among Republican and Democratic lawmakers representing New York and high-state-income-tax states in New England. 

“Anyone that is betting against Mike Lawler is making a bad bet,” Putnam County Executive Kevin Byrne told the Daily Caller. 

I’ll do whatever it takes to get things done and deliver commonsense results for the Hudson Valley. pic.twitter.com/Ks1XoZzwZf— Mike Lawler (@lawler4ny) August 27, 2026

“Mike is very bipartisan and has an independent streak on a number of issues,” Byrne continued. 

Lawler’s strategy appears to be resonating with at least some voters. A July Co/efficient poll found him leading Conley 50 percent to 45 percent, with the Republican holding a 15-point advantage among independent voters, who are largely seen as critical to his reelection bid. 

When asked whether Lawler’s independence appeals to moderate democrats and independents in the district, Byrne said, “Absolutely, 100 percent.”

In the Sunshine State, Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna has risen to national prominence through her online prowess and firebrand political profile, taking on government institutions, congressional leadership, and even members of her own party. Now, the two-term lawmaker is facing a serious Democratic challenge in a district where her anti-establishment brand is being put to the test.

Luna rose to prominence as the Hispanic outreach coordinator for Turning Point USA and later carried that notoriety to Congress. Despite losing the congressional race for her current seat in 2020, she returned two years later and has held the district since.

The Florida lawmaker will face Leela Gray in November, a retired Army brigadier general and lawyer who has attracted national Democratic support. The race would ordinarily be considered a long shot for Democrats given the district’s Republican tilt, but recent polling suggests Gray has at least made the contest competitive.

Luna’s greatest political strength may prove to be a vulnerability: The lawmaker has spent years cultivating a national profile as a Republican willing to fight the establishment. Now she’s working to convince voters that her combative brand is better than that of a moderate Democrat with broad appeal.

Ohio Republican Max Miller was supposed to be running for reelection in one of the safest Republican seats in the country. Instead, a bitter family dispute and a series of serious allegations have turned his race into a newfound pickup opportunity for Democrats.

Emily Moreno, Miller’s ex-wife, has accused him of domestic violence involving both herself and their daughter, allegations the Buckeye State lawmaker denies. Her father, Republican Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, has called on Miller to resign and end his reelection campaign.

Miller’s Democratic challenger, Brook Park City Councilman Brian Poindexter, was considered a long shot in the solidly Republican district until mounting legal and political troubles gave Democrats an opening they otherwise wouldn’t have found.

New polling shows Poindexter leading Miller 47 percent to 33 percent among likely voters, giving national Democrats enough evidence that the race could become competitive. (RELATED: What Do Trump’s 2024 Swing Voters Want From Him Now?)

However, Poindexter has faced concerning allegations of his own — though not nearly on the level of domestic abuse. He was recently accused of swallowing a bag of cocaine during a previous traffic stop and slapping another spectator at a Cleveland Indians game after the individual made comments about how Poindexter ate a hot dog, according to the Washington Free Beacon.

As a father and husband, I can tell you the last two years have been pure hell for my wife Bridget, our daughter Emily, me, and our entire family in the aftermath of Emily's divorce.It has been horrific to watch this play out in full public view, all while knowing an innocent…— Bernie Moreno (@berniemoreno) August 2, 2026

The mounting allegations prompted the House Ethics Committee to open an investigation into Miller.

Miller’s biggest hurdle to reelection may be that the Republican Party itself is divided over whether he can still win the seat. While Trump has reportedly warned Miller that his reelection prospects are dim and Republican senators including Jon Husted and Tim Sheehy have urged him to step aside, House Speaker Mike Johnson has defended the Ohio lawmaker, calling him a “great member of Congress.”

For Miller, his path back to Congress might depend less on repairing his standing among his Republican colleagues in Washington than on convincing Republican voters at home that the allegations surrounding his family life should not determine his political future. 

Michigan Republican Tom Barrett is facing a different kind of challenge; he’s a freshman member of Congress running in a district that was already competitive, but Barrett is hedging his bets on his easygoing persona and willingness to buck Trump to keep him on the Hill.

A former Michigan state senator and 22-year Army veteran, Barrett won the seat in 2024 after losing a 2022 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin. 

This time around, he’s facing progressive organizer Will Lawrence, who emerged from a crowded Democratic primary in August and is being backed by national Democrats as they target the seat. The race is already considered a toss-up, with recent Democratic-aligned polling showing Lawrence holding a narrow advantage over Barrett.

“It’s a 50-50 seat. There’s no two ways about it,” Jason Roe, a political advisor for the Congressman, told the Caller.

Nonetheless, Roe emphasized the inroads the Congressman has made in the district and the lawmaker’s charm, saying, “I think one of the secrets to his success is he’s just such a likable guy.”

Barrett has increasingly leaned into his independence from Trump, backing a War Powers Resolution led by Democrats in the lower chamber. The freshman member has also carved out his own position in the growing fight over data centers, arguing that local communities should have the final say on where the facilities are built, despite having previously supported the technology. 

The freshman congressman recently introduced legislation to protect local zoning authority over data centers, even as President Donald Trump has emerged as one of the industry’s most vocal defenders.

“Will Lawrence, while a very good progressive organizer, is a very flawed general election candidate,” Roe told the Caller.

The progressive activist rose to prominence as the co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, a progressive climate organization. Lawrence was arrested in 2013 after chaining himself to the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline site.

Nonetheless, Lawrence is betting that a national Democratic environment, along with his progressive economic message, can overcome the conventional wisdom that his politics make him a difficult candidate for a swing district. Democratic leaders and other Democrats have questioned his electability, while Lawrence has embraced the criticism and made issues such as affordability, corporate power, and data centers central to his campaign.

This ragtag group of Republican lawmakers, facing some of the toughest races this November, highlights the wide-ranging approaches campaigns are taking in the midterm elections. Candidates are looking for creative ways to hold onto their seats during an election year widely seen as advantageous for Democratic candidates across the country.

Ultimately, they will have to convince voters to look beyond the national political environment and give individual Republicans another term. Whether they can do so will determine whether some of the party’s most vulnerable members can survive past November.
news.summary: ‘It’s a 50-50 seat’
news.author: Adriel Perez,Adriel Perez-Gonzalez

news.title: Hunter Biden Claims Kamala Harris 'Isn't a Very Good Politician' as He Says Ex-Veep Wasn't 'Loyal to a Fault' to His Father Joe
news.text:
Hunter Biden had some harsh words for his father's replacement on the 2024 Democratic ticket, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

Joe Biden's son has been accused of "throwing Kamala Harris under the bus" after the then-president was pushed aside by his own party in hopes the now ex-veep could defeat Donald Trump.Hunter Biden Holds Little Back in Evaluating Kamala Harris' Political SavvyHunter, who has been on a media blitz lately, sat down for a wide-ranging interview with Zeteo Editor-in-Chief Mehdi Hasan all about President Biden's time in office.

At one point, the host pressed the 56-year-old on his repeated criticism of Harris and her political divorce from his dad, asking whether Hunter ever questioned her loyalty to Joe.

"Let me just state it exactly clearly. I think that she was loyal to my father, [but] I don’t think that she was loyal to a fault, however," Hunter replied.When Hasan asked him to detail how she was disloyal, Hunter merely chuckled and said, "That's between her and me."

Hunter's comments may have surprised some, especially Harris, but he proudly boasted that he "ain’t running for anything" and he can "say whatever the f‑‑‑ I want."

He then added that Harris has a "deep, rich future in politics" but would not be the frontrunner if he decides to run again in 2028, flatly assessing, "She's not a very good politician."Joe Biden's Relationship with Kamala Harris Has Turned ColdAs Radar has reported, the relationship between Joe and Harris has turned tense since both left office – something she confessed to in her behind-the-scenes memoir, 107 Days, writing that she was saddened by his apparent change in attitude toward her.

"My feelings for him were grounded in warmth and loyalty, but they had become complicated, over time, with hurt and disappointment," she wrote.

Harris claimed the Joe Biden she knew during their first campaign had turned into a different person after he won.

"After warmly welcoming us into the Biden family at the beginning of the campaign, there seemed to be a change of temperature after the election," she wrote.'People Hate Joe Biden'Harris previously detailed that after Joe withdrew from the 2024 campaign, she spent the first few days as the new Democratic candidate getting her feet wet and finding her own voice. 

At the start, her standard stump speech would include glowing remarks about her former boss, but her advisers quickly suggested she change her tone on him.

"I spent the first third of my remarks effusively praising him before I launched into my own campaign speech," Harris wrote in her book. "I would do that for several weeks until my campaign strategists urged me to stop: 'It's time this campaign was about you.'"

However, President Obama's 2008 campaign manager, David Plouffe, who was now working to help elect Harris, put it more bluntly when he told her point-blank: "People hate Joe Biden."Joe Biden's Turn to Criticize Kamala HarrisFor his part, Joe's camp rushed to defend the former president after Harris released her tell-all, and even threw some shade of their own at her.

Presidential expert Leon Wagener said: "Kamala has a chip on her shoulder, and she's been told by everybody in the party to keep her mouth shut or 'we'll bury you.'

"Everyone knows there is a deep well of dislike and distrust between them – and it's going to be an all-out war if she talks and the Biden team goes after her."

Political reporter Mark Halperin claimed that even before the book, Joe was preparing to bite back: "If the Biden people feel threatened, you will hear stories about Kamala Harris as vice president that will not make her look good.

"I'm telling you, if Joe Biden feels threatened, if his people feel threatened by her, this is going to escalate in a big way."
news.summary: Joe Biden's son has been accused of throwing Kamala Harris under the bus after the then-president was pushed off the 2024 ticket.
news.author: Daniel Gura

news.title: What Is Iran's Boiling Point? We May Be Very Close to Finding Out.
news.text:
I can't say I remember all of my high school chemistry and physics education, but I do remember the concept about water boiling. Under normal atmospheric pressure, 212 degrees is the magic temperature for it to begin bubbling off into steam in earnest. But if you can pressurize the container holding the water, doubling its surroundings in atmospheric pressure, you get an additional 36 degrees of heat before boiling begins. That's why cars and trucks for a very long time have had pressurized cooling systems for engines. Don't worry, I'm not going to geek out on science for the rest of this column. I bring it up in order show that cars and water have a very symbiotic relationship, provided that they're used in the right way. And when they're not, as is happening with increasing frequency inside Iran, we're about to see what happens when pressure reaches its critical point. An important sequence of events took place in the Middle East in the last week, and much of it was very predictable based upon economic conditions deteriorating rapidly inside Iran that we covered last week. Without any revenue, gasoline, grain, or weapons flowing into the Islamic Republic, and nothing to generate revenue leaving, the IRGC could not stand still and starve along with 93 million Iranians. The status quo of the blockade with the addition of further sanctions rolled out in Operation Economic Outcast was not sustainable. They had to lash out in order to change the equation. The last straw for the regime? De-mining the Strait of Hormuz. As President Trump is fond of saying, Iran's Navy is gone. What they had left was speedboats with machine guns tied to them. Most of those are gone now, too. But late last week, the IRGC began scrambling together a ragtag group of naval volunteers into whatever they could find that would float, and fashion a few more mines to begin the process of closing the Strait anew. There were reports that the Iranians wanted to deploy rockets with mines as payloads and drop them into the Strait, as absurd as that sounds. Of course, Centcom had a pretty good idea they would try something, and unlike Iran, our Navy and Air Force have the ability to watch them. On Sunday, targets on Larak Island, one of the channel islands in the Strait of Hormuz, the same island the IRGC envisioned would be the proverbial toll booth collecting fees from tankers and freighters, were destroyed. And according to several open source reports in Israel and around the region, it was a direct hit. How do we know? The Iranians immediately launched nine missiles in response at...Jordan. 

The Islamic Republic’s massive ballistic missile response tonight may indicate the U.S. strike on Larak Island was far more devastating than initially acknowledged.Channel 14, citing sources, says the strike killed dozens of IRGC personnel and wounded nearly 100 others. Those… pic.twitter.com/LiqUclS6wN— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) August 30, 2026

Eight of the nine missiles were intercepted and destroyed, and one was far enough off course it was not a threat to anything except scorpions. President Trump expected Iran to pop off, and in keeping with his motto to hit ten times as hard if Iran went kinetic, two waves of strikes hit targets up and down the southern coast of Iran.

The President, in his response to Iran, said there is no more deal on the table. Howie Mandel is not in the Oval Office with a bevy of young ladies with briefcases and a mysterious banker on the phone. His banker is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and there is no more offer. There is either surrender or more pain and suffering. On social media, Trump gave this AI video as a warning to the Iranians not to escalate after this response.

He later told Fox News' Trey Yingst that if the regime launched again after this, he would flatten them.

We gave them a lot of chances!" 👀If Iran fires back: "They'll be hit much… pic.twitter.com/FlG21HSRJ2— Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) September 1, 2026

Did Iran take their beating and stand down? Nah. They found 14 more rockets and fired...at Jordan again. Why Jordan? We have a military base there. We still do. Ten of thirteen rockets were once again intercepted and destroyed mid-air, and three were wide right of the uprights and wiped out more desert fauna. What about the 14th rocket, you ask? Well, it went up, and then came down on an Iranian house that was full of people conducting a wedding ceremony. 

🚨🇮🇷 Breaking: Four people were killed and over 60 injured after an IRGC missile misfired at an Iranian wedding. pic.twitter.com/TeXqVpKTia— C14 News | EN (@c14english) September 1, 2026

The regime blamed the tragedy on U.S. strikes while simultaneously admitting that a telecommunications tower was also struck. The tower and the house, by the way, were not near each other. This is what's left of the tower. 

The Kuhestak telecommunications tower has been destroyed. https://t.co/XJ2xrgrO40 pic.twitter.com/H697ACmAPW— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) September 1, 2026

President Trump, to pour salt in the wound, said the U.S. had been watching Iranians build this tower, which would help restore their radar system and track vessels in the Strait once again. We waited until they had basically rebuilt the thing — investing all the time, money, and energy, and then we blew it up. It's sad bordering on the pathetic, but after everyone in the Middle East hearing about the menacing power of the vaunted Iranian Navy for decades, this literally is what constitutes the regime navy this week. 

🚨 An embarrassing video shows the Islamic Republic sending Basij volunteers in fishing boats and cheap, low-tech speedboats into the Persian Gulf to confront American warships.The volunteers wave Islamic Republic flags as they head toward the Strait of Hormuz in small…— The Iran Watcher (@TheIranWatcher) August 30, 2026

As of last night, the promised intensified third round of strikes had not begun. They certainly could be imminent, as it would be in keeping with what President Trump said multiple times in the last few days. But perhaps something else may be on the horizon. We'll come back to that in a bit. I mentioned about cars, water, and pressure, and how Iran is about to become one giant science experiment. Let's begin with water. As scarce as gasoline appears to be in populated areas, in the more rural regions, water is even harder to come by.

Water deliveries have all but stopped since the war began, and you have to walk miles to get it.

Forget about plumbing and irrigation. Water showing up just under once a month for entire villages? How long is that supposed to be sustainable? news.title: Dem megadonor among 400 Jewish Michiganders labeled AIPAC insiders for denouncing El-Sayed's leftist campaign
news.text: More than 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders are backing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and warning that they feel "threatened and alienated" by leftist candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his political allies. Prominent Democratic donor Rob Orley, a senior advisor for O2 Investments, is among the signatories. He previously donated tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic campaigns, according to FEC campaign filings — but now he and other prominent Jewish leaders are ditching El-Sayed for Republican candidate Mike Rogers. "Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles," a letter signed by Orley and hundreds of others stated. "If El-Sayed were to win the general election in this important swing state, we fear the far-left and anti-Jewish elements in the Democratic Party would become dominant, including in the imminent 2028 presidential race," the letter continues. "We cannot allow him to become the Democratic standard-bearer or Michigan’s senator." Fox News Digital reached out to O2 Investments for comment. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS The letter includes signatures from some of the most prominent members of Michigan's Jewish community, including Robert Gordon, the former president of Temple Israel, the state's largest Jewish congregation, which was the site of an antisemitic attack in March. Shayna Levine, the daughter of the leading rabbi at Temple Israel; David Propis, cantor of Congregation Shaarey Zedek; Laurence Deitch, who served as a University of Michigan regent; and Hannan Lis, a Weight Watchers executive, have also signed the letter declaring that they feel "threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed." But former Rep. Andy Levin, who is Jewish, is claiming that opposition to El-Sayed among Jewish Democrats is a minority view and that his old foe, the American Israel Political Action Committee, is really driving the letter. Levin lost his 2022 primary bid to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., after AIPAC spent more than $4 million in the primary race against him. "It's not a surprise to me," Levin said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The people I know associated with it are all long-time AIPAC insiders and supporters." Levin added that AIPAC "represents a distinctly minority position about Israel and Palestine within the Jewish community." Levin, who was first elected to Congress in 2018 to replace his late father Sander Levin, gave his endorsement to El-Sayed in November 2025. "I am overwhelmed like literally every day except Shabbat — our sabbath on Saturday — with the incoming I get from Jewish people, young people, middle-aged people, older people, who are so mad about an effort like this and who want to do everything they can to make sure Abdul El-Sayed wins the election on November 3rd, that this U.S. Senate seat stays democratic, and that we do everything we can to save and expand our democracy," Levin continued. However, attorney Daniel Cherrin, who signed the letter, told Fox News Digital that he has not attended an AIPAC event since college more than 30 years ago. Cherrin said he has tremendous respect for Levin, whom he has known for years, and previously worked with Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit and Wayne County. Although he considers El-Sayed a "good" person, Cherrin said he cannot overlook the movement backing his candidacy. "I am very concerned about the movement that is behind Abdul, and for the safety of my community, I don't feel safe in that environment with the people that are standing in support of him," Cherrin told Fox News Digital. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN "They don't understand the impact that their words and their actions is having on me and my children and my neighbors," Cherrin said. "And so, for that, I am very worried about should he be elected what that means for all those that are trying to advance his candidacy." Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who has called Orthodox Jews inbreds and said America deserved 9/11, has been a top surrogate for El-Sayed's campaign. Over the past week, El-Sayed has attempted to distance himself from the social media influencer, suggesting that people focusing on his affiliation with Piker are "missing the boat." Levin, who has condemned Piker's antisemitic falsehoods about the Oct. 7 attack, agreed with El-Sayed that too much focus is on Piker. He then argued that the Democratic National Committee received very little pushback for inviting Piker to stream during the 2024 Democratic National Convention, giving then-Vice President and Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris an opportunity to reach Piker's audience. Piker did not endorse Harris because of the Biden administration's policy in the Gaza war. "So I'm not accepting Hasan Piker, but look in the mirror, sister," Levin said. "When it's a guy named Abdul with a guy named Hasan, you're blowing up about it and covering it massively. When it was not an Arab American or a Muslim who campaigned with him or did whatever Kamala Harris did, literally no one asked her a single question about it." Last month, El-Sayed said he had "no plans" to continue campaigning with Piker. Roslyn Schindler attends Congregation T'chiyah, which is a progressive Reform synagogue that touts its support for Black Lives Matter, and transgender rights, with Levin. A daughter of Holocaust survivors, Schindler has lived in the metro Detroit area for 50 years and taught Holocaust studies at Wayne State University. She shared with Fox News Digital that she has supported El-Sayed well before his primary victory, and that the Democratic Party is in need of a "major shake-up," citing El-Sayed's support for progressive policies like Medicare for All and getting money out of politics. "I am certainly not an anti-Zionist, as many Jews who don't support Abdul think we are, but I am a committed Jew," Schindler told Fox News Digital. "I'm a committed Democrat. I believe that the Democratic Party should be a large tent, so to speak, that includes all members of that party, no matter what their perspective." Fox News Digital asked Schindler for her thoughts on El-Sayed's affiliation with Piker and whether there is a place in the Democratic Party for people who follow his ideology. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER "As a Jew, I certainly don't want anyone to be anti-Semitic. I don't want anyone to be anti-Muslim. I don't want anyone to be anti-LGBTQ, and the list goes on," Schindler said. "Is that realistic? Probably not. Do I want those people to be part of the Democratic Party? It's not really for me to want. It is what it is. They'll either be part of it or they won't." "But I do believe there is enough traction within the Jewish community at large to counter anti-Semitism, and that's across the board," Schindler continued. But Cherrin said the fact that his family has to pass security officers guarding synagogues and temples is evidence to him that the Jewish community at large can't tackle antisemitism by itself. "It's not about AIPAC for me," Cherrin said. "It is about it is about how are we protecting the sanctity of the Jewish community in Michigan and frankly and across the country with all these other races that are out there." "People within the Jewish community, who typically identify as Democrats, don't feel comfortable voting for the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate and are looking for a place to channel their frustration. That should not be discounted," Cherrin continued. Cherrin pushed for both Rogers and El-Sayed to continue to reach out to Jewish community members outside of politics to get a "real pulse" on what Jewish voters are thinking. "Abdul is grateful for the good conversations he’s had with Jewish leaders across Michigan, and he’ll continue to be actively engaged with communities to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate, and put a much-needed check on Trump’s reckless agenda," a spokesperson for El-Sayed's campaign said in a statement to Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Rogers, who previously served in Congress for 15 years, said he appreciates the growing support from the Jewish community — especially those crossing party lines to back his bid for U.S. Senate. "As antisemitism rises and Jewish families worry for their safety, it’s critical that we have leaders who will confront hatred — not inflame it," Rogers said in a statement. "That’s where my opponent and I couldn’t be more different." "Abdul El-Sayed fans the flames of antisemitism. We’re fighting to extinguish it," Rogers continued. Although for progressive Jewish Democrats like Levin and Schindler, President Donald Trump and his MAGA allies like Rogers are the biggest threat to democracy. "We have a chance to protect our Democracy by keeping this U.S. Senate seat democratic and expanding our democracy, by, for the first time, having, uh, electing a Muslim to the U.S. Senate," Levin said. "Most Jews that I know so believe in this democratic experiment, this Democratic project called America." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And it's about damn time that Muslims had a senator and there's a brilliant person running here in Michigan who we can elect to be the first one. Will he do exactly what a Jewish person would do or something? No, but he will be someone we could talk to and who will be a great representative for all of Michigan and for the Arab American and Muslim communities in particular," Levin said.
news.summary: Over 400 Michigan Jewish Democrats signed a letter backing Mike Rogers, but former Rep. Andy Levin claims AIPAC is really driving the effort.
