news.title: Even Jesse Watters fell for this handsome doctor’s rizz. Could Michigan’s El-Sayed shift the balance of power in America?
news.text:
Conservatives keep falling for the far-left’s charm offensive. First it was Donald Trump, beaming up at a stoic-looking Zohran Mamdani, then the newly elected mayor of New York City, at a White House visit that confounded Fox News and Mamdani’s opponents alike — even contributing to a Republican dropping out of the gubernatorial race against Gov. Kathy Hochul.

Last week it was Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the winner of a hard-fought Michigan Senate primary, charming the socks off of Jesse Watters, the impish Fox News primetime host who took on the epidemiologist in a combative but also almost jovial interview where the two sparred on a wide range of topics and aimed sharp jabs at each other — but with a seeming bro-code respect.

“I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn’t like him, but I do,” admitted Watters on The Five after the interview aired. “I think he’d be a terrible senator and he’s a little bit of a lunatic…But at least he’s not your typical stiff.”

With America staring down the midterm elections in just a few months, the fate of two congressional majorities is up in the air. Just one year ago, both Republicans and Democrats seemed confident that the GOP had built a strong Senate majority in the 2024 cycle, thanks to the crushing defeat of Kamala Harris. Many expected that majority to withstand the typical headwinds that form against the president’s party in off-year elections. 

But one year, one war in the Middle East and one trade conflict with Canada later, the map for Republicans looks wildly different.

“This is not a question of if the Democrats are getting gains,” said Trevor Francis, a former GOP strategist. “It's how much, and where.”

The retirements of two Republican senators, the interference of the president in GOP primaries, and the spiraling unpopularity of the president less than two years into his second term have given Democrats a realistic path to the majority — and an El-Sayed victory in Michigan, to hold a seat currently occupied by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, is critical to that path.

But both Democrats and Republicans agree that also critical to that effort of winning a majority is running a new kind of Democratic campaign. Whether progressive, like El-Sayed and Mamdani, or centrist like Georgia’s Sen. Jon Ossoff, many Democratic campaigns operating since Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential defeat are utilizing a very different media playbook than she did — or even other Democratic House and Senate candidates were wielding in the last cycle. 

Gone are the days of avoiding Joe Rogan, Fox News, or avoiding controversy, as Ossoff revealed when he triggered a multi-day media cycle around Natalie Harp, Trump’s young aide whose relationship with the president has been questioned by some in the White House.

Emily Suttle-Braun, whose firm Doodle Moms is supporting digital fundraising for both El-Sayed’s campaign and Jocelyn Benson’s gubernatorial effort in Michigan, told The Independent that it came down to two factors when analyzing El-Sayed’s recent success: A Mamdani-like message discipline and an aggressive media-focused campaign style that meets different groups of voters where they are.

“These are candidates who have a very talented communication standard,” she said. “You can raise a lot of money, you can pay a bunch of money for ads, you can knock every door, but at the end of the day, that's that I think is what sets these candidates apart is how they communicate.”

Mentioning El-Sayed, Ossoff, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Texas Rep. James Talarico, Suttle-Braun added: “I think it's talent, and I think it's passion, right? And those two things do not always come together.”

Francis, who previously served as national communications director for the Republican National Committee, differed over whether the Watters Fox interview would be of serious benefit to El-Sayed’s campaign. He argued instead that El-Sayed should be focused on local media appearances over the conservative cable juggernaut. But he agreed that the former Wayne County health department director was a “naturally talented communicator” who “embraces conflict media” like the Fox News sphere.

“It’s less about where he shows up, but [more about] how he presents himself,” Francis told The Independent. “He is always very relatable and very authentic, and I think those are the two things that are the most important thing in any candidate.”

Francis’ advice to El-Sayed was simple: Like Mamdani, the Michigander should “make the issue the issue” and constantly pivot back to discussion of affordability.

“I think everything needs to be a pivot back to that,” he said. “Donald Trump has a unique ability of disrupting the media ecosystem, but he also is very good at redirecting the topic to where he wants it to be, and I feel like there is something to be said for Abdul's campaign to do the same thing.”

Suttle-Braun, who described herself as more moderate, concluded that El-Sayed’s campaign was also indicative of one other dynamic: The progressive left’s embrace of younger staffers and fresher political talent beyond just their selection of candidates.

“It comes down to who these campaigns are hiring, and the DSA candidates are-- they're modern, right? They're taking more risks. They're diversifying their paid media. They're putting much more money into sort of like clipping and social media and earned media than they are into like traditional paid media like TV, and that that is a bet that is really paying off for them.” 

”They're hiring agencies, consultants, strategists like myself, tech companies who are not like regurgitating the same Democratic campaign ‘rinse, repeat’-like formula,” added Suttle-Braun. “And that's really cool, by the way, to see.”
news.summary: Democratic campaigns like El-Sayed’s are embracing charisma, bravado and some ‘really cool’ strategies — and aren’t afraid to jump into the lion’s den of conservative media, strategists on both sides of the aisle tell John Bowden

news.title: Six takeaways from the Massachusetts primaries — from Markey to Neal
news.text:
Massachusetts, as it turns out, is a good state in which to be a very old Democratic incumbent.

Three Democrats who have been in office since long before the iPhone was in stores all won renomination Tuesday. Sen. Ed Markey, 80, and Reps. Richard Neal, 77, and Stephen F. Lynch, 71, are all likely to return for additional terms.

Each faced challengers who had called for a new generation of leadership. Markey coasted past Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who ran to the middle, while Neal and Lynch both fought off progressive challengers.

Markey has been in office for 50 years. Neal has represented western Massachusetts since 1989. Lynch first won election from South Boston in 2001. The state's Democrats do not seem inclined to reject their incumbents.

Here are six takeaways from the Massachusetts primary results:

1. Voters didn't care about Markey's age.

The party still scarred by former President Joe Biden's public meltdown during the 2024 campaign was not convinced that an octogenarian senator should not serve another six years.

Perhaps if Markey, 80, had faced a younger challenger with better political relationships than Moulton, he would have been in trouble in Tuesday's Democratic primary. But Moulton has spent his career challenging his party's orthodoxy and its leaders.

That record left Markey the political space he needed to paint himself as the progressive in the race, campaigning on the ideas of the future — even though he has been in Congress for 50 years.

In the waning days of the Massachusetts primary, several Democrats described Moulton as having the generational change message the party needed but being the wrong messenger to deliver it.

Markey said throughout the campaign that he would resign his seat if his advanced age left him unable to properly fulfill his Senate duties. He is now favored to win in November, which would have him serve in the Senate until he is 86 years old.

2. Moulton's trans remarks weren't forgotten.

If Massachusetts were a general election battleground state, perhaps Moulton's skepticism about trans athletes' participation in youth sports might have played better among primary voters.

But from the moment Moulton entered the race last October, Markey used his remarks questioning transgender girls' participation in girls' sports as a battering ram against him. Not only did it galvanize the LGBTQ vote for Markey, it also helped frame him as the progressive candidate.

It was the same formula that powered Markey's last primary triumph in 2020 against another younger, more moderate Democrat, Joe Kennedy III.

Moulton eventually offered a qualified apology for his remarks, which came the day after President Donald Trump won a second term in the 2024 election. But by then the state's progressive voters had heard for months from Markey and his supporters that Moulton, during tough times, was willing to toss trans people aside.

3. Dan Koh wins, thanks to Biden and Harris.

A lot of Democrats rolled their eyes when Dan Koh rolled out endorsement videos from Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Koh, who was a White House aide for Biden, was running against Tram Nguyen, a progressive state legislator, for Moulton's House seat north of Boston.

Tying one's political identity to a presidential administration a lot of Democrats would like to move past was a unique strategy. No other Democrat in a competitive primary this year had video testimonials from both Biden and Harris. (He also had a lot of help from a pro-AI super political action committee.)

The strategy worked. Koh won a relatively easy victory over Nguyen and four other candidates. In a heavily Democratic district, he is all but certain to enter Congress in January as a legacy of the Biden administration.

4. Stephen Lynch and Richie Neal hang on

Markey was not the only old guy to hang on Tuesday. Neal and Lynch both fended off younger challengers for their House seats.

Unlike Markey, Neal and Lynch both faced progressive upstarts. And while both won by margins closer than they have achieved in previous races, they are both likely to return to Congress for another two years.

Massachusetts has not elected a Republican to any of its congressional seats since 1994. As long as that remains the case — and it is widely expected to — five of the nine members of the Massachusetts House delegation next year will be 63 or older. Both senators will be 77 or older. And efforts by young challengers to oust the state's older incumbents have failed time after time.

5. The pollsters got one right.

The polling industry has gotten a lot of grief lately after Democratic primary results were way off from the forecasts of the final surveys in Michigan and Wisconsin, followed by a big upset in the Florida Senate race.

In Massachusetts, Big Polling got it right.

Emerson College and the University of New Hampshire released polls in the final week before the primary showing Markey as getting more than 60% of the vote — blowout numbers.

They turned out to be right on target.

Getting the numbers right is something of a triumph for pollsters as they head into the final general election sprint in election battlegrounds.

Ambitious Democrats are already looking toward 2030 and '32.

The next two Massachusetts Senate contests could feature a pileup of ambitious Democrats from competing wings of the party.

The state's Senate races in 2030, when Sen. Elizabeth Warren, now 77, would face reelection, and 2032, when Markey's next term would end, are likely to be open-seat contests.

Markey said in July that the term he was running for now would be his last. Warren would be 81 in 2030.

Massachusetts has no shortage of Democrats who have been eyeing upcoming Senate openings. Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Jake Auchincloss have barely disguised their interest in the seats. Mayor Michelle Wu of Boston is a popular progressive. Marty Walsh, the former Boston mayor who served as Biden's labor secretary, could also mount a run.

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

news.text:
Democrats are in a quandary over the Supreme Court. Every four years, they've warned their voters that electing a Republican president will lead to more conservative Supreme Court justices. And yet since Ronald Reagan's election in 1980 through today, they've lost more presidential elections than they've won. Maybe the voters are telling Democrats something. Maybe Americans don't want the court packed with Sonia Sotomayors who make up or rewrite the laws as they see fit.

So now the left is angry over the tilt of the court, which has six conservatives and three liberals.

Why? Because elections have consequences. Sorry, this is the price you pay for nominating Michael Dukakis, John Kerry, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. They aren't exactly hanging around anywhere near the 50-yard line on political ideology.

Now we have Democrats divided on what to do next. Many want Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Elizabeth Warren to be their next presidential nominee. There's no learning curve here.

In the meantime, while Donald Trump is still president, they want urgent action. On the one hand, the democratic socialists want to abolish the highest court of the land. What they want to replace it with is anyone's guess.

Other party leaders want to pack the court with four new liberal justices. Franklin Roosevelt tried this court-packing scheme in 1937, and voters rebelled.

But here they go again. On Sunday, Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) raised this possibility and disgracefully played the race card when asked about the Supreme Court's recent decisions. He accused Republicans of taking "this country back ... to those rulings of Justice Taney that said, 'No Black man has any right that a white man must respect.'" He was referring to Supreme Court Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the infamous 1857 Dred Scott opinion just before the Civil War.

Does he even know that for 100 years after the Civil War, Democrats were the party of segregation?

What's deeply troubling about this war on the Supreme Court is that this is the institution that is the final check against runaway mob-rule democracy that can trample the rights of the minority. That minority could be Blacks, Hispanics, gays, immigrants or disabled people. They don't seem to understand that pure majority-rule democracy is, as the old saying goes, two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner.

Pure democracy only goes your way until you no longer have 50% plus one voters on your side. Clyburn is right that there have been occasions, like the one from 1857 that he mentioned, when the court has made egregiously wrong decisions. But mostly, the court gets it right. It's not clear how stacking the court — on the left or the right — could make for more just decisions.

This is why Republicans are so wrong to try to abolish the filibusters in the Senate. We always want to make it HARDER, not easier, to pass new edicts that impair our freedoms.

I, personally, would have no problem expanding the Supreme Court to 12 justices if it could be done in a fair, nonpartisan way. I also strongly support a mandatory retirement age of 75 for all future justices on the court.

But to overly politicize — or, worse, do away with — the Supreme Court and allow Congress to have the last word on the constitutionality of new laws is a dangerous proposition. James Madison once famously described the judiciary as a "bulwark" of our liberties. Hopefully, we will never give up this most important check and balance on runaway government power.

news.title: JD Vance’s attacks on Democrats sound eerily familiar
news.text:
It could be a stump speech for almost any Democrat running this year: Voters in the November midterms should repudiate divisive politicians, elect leaders of good character and root out fraud.

But those are the arguments Vice President JD Vance is using to attack Democrats.

While campaigning for Republican candidates over the past few weeks, Vance has repeatedly leveled attacks on their opponents that sound almost eerily like a critique of his own boss.

This may be partly due to the audience. Vance's other aim in these speeches, aside from boosting GOP voter enthusiasm, is to raise his profile ahead of an expected 2028 campaign of his own. His talking points are more for the MAGA faithful, who really believe that Democrats are doing all of this.

It may also be a way to inoculate Trump from those points of criticism. If everyone is arguing that their opponents are corrupt or crazy, then some low-information voters may simply tune out all sides.

Whatever his aims, the extent to which Vance’s attacks on Democrats echo criticism of Trump is remarkable.

Divisive politicians

At a rally for Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Detroit on Monday, Vance argued that “there's something about” Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed “that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today.”

“And it’s people who see themselves not as citizens of a common nation fighting for every single person — whether they’re Jewish or Christian, whether they’re white or Black or brown — but see themselves as fighting for one group at the expense of others, and that is how, ladies and gentlemen, you destroy the United States of America,” he added.

As a reminder, Trump denied or delayed disaster aid to several Democratic-led states. According to former aides, he considered whether Californians hit by wildfires had voted for him before approving aid. The administration also acknowledged in a court filing that it canceled $7.6 billion in clean energy grants solely because the recipients were located in states that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. Vance himself has argued that America is “not just an idea” and that Americans whose ancestors fought in the Civil War have “a hell of a lot more claim over America than the people who say they don’t belong.”

Americans have noticed all of this: An August poll by YouGov found that 60% of U.S. citizens said the country had become more divided under Trump.

‘Good character’

In July, Vance ended a speech in Milwaukee by calling for Americans to “send people to Washington who are of good character.”

Trump was convicted of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal hush money payments. A civil jury found him liable for sexually abusing and defaming E. Jean Carroll. And a New York court ordered him to pay $2 million and dissolved the Trump Foundation over misuse of charitable funds.

Again, Americans have noticed. In a Gallup poll in December, only 30% of U.S. adults said that Trump “is honest and trustworthy.”

‘Send the fraudsters to prison’

At the July speech in Milwaukee, Vance called Democrats “the pro-fraud party” that is “sending your tax money to the fraudsters,” while Republicans are “trying to save your money and send the fraudsters to prison.”

Trump's own record includes being found civilly liable for fraud in New York over inflated financial statements. The Trump Organization — though not Trump personally — was convicted in 2022 of 17 felonies involving a long-running tax fraud scheme. In 2011, Trump and his co-defendants agreed to return millions of dollars in deposits after buyers in Trump SoHo said they were misled by inflated sales figures. And Trump agreed to pay $25 million to settle fraud lawsuits brought by students of his Trump University real estate courses.

In his second term, Trump has pardoned Trevor Milton, the founder of an electric-truck company who misled investors about its technology; Todd and Julie Chrisley, reality TV stars who used false documents to obtain bank loans; Lawrence Duran, who orchestrated a $205 million scheme that billed Medicare for unnecessary or nonexistent mental health services; and former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich, who was convicted on charges that included attempting to sell Barack Obama’s Senate seat. The list of the more than 1,600 people that Trump has granted clemency in his second term is full of similar cases.

‘Crazy leadership’

In a May speech in Kansas City, Missouri, Vance urged supporters to “vote against the crazy leadership in Washington, D.C.” In June, he told Fox News anchor Laura Ingraham that “the only sane party left is the Republican Party.” And in June, he told another Fox host he doesn't know why Democrats “can’t just find normal, well-adjusted candidates.”

Among other things, Trump posted artificial-intelligence-generated images and videos depicting himself as a king, as the pope and as a fighter pilot dumping excrement on protesters. He also posted an image that appeared to show him as a Christlike healer. He initially refused to rule out using military force to acquire Greenland, suggested Canada should become the 51st state, renamed Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico in government documents and signed an executive order promising to restore “shower freedom.”

In short, Vance’s call for “normal, well-adjusted candidates” is a particularly awkward message for a vice president serving one Donald J. Trump.

news.text: Massachusetts Democrats rewarded incumbency in marquee primaries Tuesday, but the clearest message came in the state’s generational showdown, with 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey routing moderate Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, after Moulton argued it was time for the party to "pass the torch." Tuesday night's results underscored Democratic dominance in the deep-blue state rather than a single ideological sweep. Voters backed established incumbents across the party’s factions and selected a Biden-Harris-backed former White House aide in the closely watched open-seat contest to take over Moulton's House seat after he abandoned it to run for Senate. Meanwhile, Republicans failed to nominate House candidates in four districts — the first, second, fifth and seventh — while only fielding write-ins for the blue stronghold's secretary of state race. Markey’s victory over the more moderate Moulton, however, stood out as the night’s clearest win for the party’s progressive wing. "Another w for our movement!" Moulton highlighted the difficult battle he faced trying to unseat a longtime incumbent like Markey following his concession, but said the effort was not for nothing, noting "we started conversations that needed to happen" and adding that he is "confident ... others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn." Markey faced attacks during the campaign over his far-left positions, including his support for transgender athletes' participation in women's sports, but the progressive bona fides of the Massachusetts lawmaker, who has represented the state in Congress for nearly five decades, were not a significant enough sticking point for voters to abandon him. news.title: Maga's worst nightmare: a child-free, unmarried female president
news.text:
Welcome to Trump’s America, The i Paper’s World Insight series presenting the sharpest, deepest thinking on an era-defining shift in history and politics, investigating how Donald Trump and his administration have changed the US and the world – and where we go from here.

• $120,000 should be a great salary. In these US states, it isn’t• ‘We never changed, Trump did’: Maga’s insurgency against its own leader• The more America spends on healthcare, the sicker it gets

“Don’t be weird about this, even though I know all of you will be”. This is how American Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, aged 36 and reportedly newly single, began her announcement on Instagram that she was freezing her eggs with the hope of having a family in the future. True to form, as arguably the most social media-fluent politician of her generation, she recorded the entire process online, filming herself injecting medication while talking politics and policy.

At a time when Republican efforts to increasingly restrict women’s reproductive choices are an ongoing battle, and in a country where millions cannot afford access to basic healthcare, egg freezing is rich political terrain. By telling the world she is exercising control over her fertility to accommodate her career, AOC is further testing the murky and unforgiving waters of being a woman in politics.

When one right-wing commentator lamented AOC for trying to push the “lie” that women “can have it all”, she clapped back: “Maybe in life you can’t have everything, but here’s the secret, you can have a hell of a lot”.

Having “a lot” in AOC’s book may well mean the presidency. Indeed, many have taken this announcement to be a soft-launch bid for the Oval Office. But could America ever vote for a child-free and single female president?

The motherhood penalty

“There’s a double, triple, quadruple standard for women in politics,” says Dr Emma Long, director of the Arthur Miller Institute for American Studies at the University of East Anglia. “They somehow have to meet all of these impossible criteria that are, at least in part, rooted in traditional notions of what and who women should be.”

This unattainable criteria is a stubborn, long list, for mothers and non-mothers alike. They are expected to be both tough and nice but not too tough or too nice. They are critiqued for how they look and dress in a way their male counterparts simply aren’t.Inevitably, women with children face additional logistical hurdles (which isn’t to say that women without children don’t face additional, different hurdles). They are accused of not being committed enough to either their family or their job, while often being asked: “Who’s looking after the kids?” A Pew poll from 2024 found 48 per cent of voters see having young children at home as a disadvantage for female candidates, while just 7 per cent see it as a disadvantage for male candidates.

Yet for many American voters, research has historically shown that they would rather female politicians be mothers than not – a penalty that, again, male politicians simply haven’t faced. I had to google if Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, another young Democrat expected to run in 2028, even had a partner or children, proving how little this is considered in the discourse around him.

Meanwhile, no one seemed remotely bothered that New York City’s youngest Mayor, Zohran Mamdani – cut from a very similar cloth to AOC and who campaigned on the affordability crisis for working families – wasn’t a father. Interestingly, however, The Guardian cites research that found “two-thirds of Americans disagreed that not having biological children was a hindrance in a president” and “even among Republicans, only 15 per cent agreed”. Yet, tellingly, this does not differentiate by gender.

The spectacle of the First Family

A more recent poll from Pew found that 53 per cent think the country would be worse off if women had fewer children – up 6 per cent than a year earlier. And one survey from the Women and Politics Institute at American University reports respondents had a very set idea of what a female president would look like: “The first female president is imagined narrowly, a married Democratic mother under 65 with political experience, and voters say she must be both ‘tough’ and ‘likeable.’” Which sounds like AOC – except for the marriage and the children. Has AOC revealed her egg freezing, not just to admit her plans to run, but to let the world know she wants a family, to prove her maternal instincts to the country? “There may be a political penalty for doing this,” she says in one video. But then again, there may have also been a penalty if she had kept her ambition for a family private.

Historically, people have been suspicious of women who don’t have children. “They’re somehow not seen as trustworthy,” says Jennifer Piscopo, professor of gender and politics and director of the Gender Institute at Royal Holloway, University of London.

The sentiment is particularly true for Republican voters. Another Pew poll from 2024 found that 59 per cent of Trump supporters vs 19 per cent of Biden supporters believe it is better if people prioritise marriage and children. In both parties, more men think this than women. When JD Vance called Democratic politicians a “bunch of childless cat ladies with miserable lives” in 2021, a vicious backlash ensued. However, it also showed these tired stereotypes being resurrected and weaponised, revealing just how much the Maga movement would use the reinforcement of gender norms as political arsenal.

America, Long says, is still “a small ‘c’ conservative nation” and “Republicans are the natural majority party”. Family life remains a core tenet of the American right. “As the family goes, so goes the nation,” Ronald Reagan, Trump’s favourite modern president, famously said in 1985. The First Family has also been a huge part of America’s cultural landscape – and this has never been more true than under Trump, with his children increasingly benefitting from their father’s power.

Modern America

Yet, America is in a time of flux: traditional drivers of family life are slipping. The nation is currently experiencing record-low fertility rates, and more people are choosing to be child-free, which by some counts, amounts to potentially 60 million child-free voters. Fewer people follow Christianity than ever before. In 1950, 87 per cent of Americans claimed to be Christian; today that number is somewhere between 60-68 per cent. Add to the mix that some research suggests America will be a white minority nation by 2045. It’s not insignificant that AOC isn’t just a single woman without kids – she’s a Latina single woman without kids. Every way you slice it, she embodies a new America.

In light of this decline in a faith and family-first approach, the lack of children represents a existential threat to some voters. That is spurring on calls among Maga republicans for a return to an “idealised” former. The rise of the tradwife and pronatalism movements under Donald Trump are no coincidence. We’re witnessing a violent crackdown on immigration and a sometimes ridiculous, and sometimes sinister, display of hypermasculinity. All these things reflect a profound fear about what a candidate like AOC could represent.

Yet for all his bluster, Trump is doing terribly in the polls: fuel prices are soaring, and the country is in a war nobody wants. Could a backlash to Trump vote in a new type of president, and have we ever seen anything like this before?

“We have simply not had a presidency that has so profoundly restricted American politics, restructured the federal government and transformed and broken democratic norms,” says Piscopo. “So there is no precedent for what that response looks like”.

But, she says, maybe because this is uncharted territory, voters could be more open to new ideas. “I think a savvy actor like AOC sees that perhaps this is the chance for a non-traditional candidate, an authentic candidate, a candidate who’s long been a voice for things that are different from the Trump and Maga vision of the world, to pick up all the very upset voters. The opportunities would not be better in more traditional politics when everyone looks like Joe Biden. She should be thinking, ‘This is perhaps the moment for an overcorrection, and I can be that candidate.’”

Long disagrees. Her answer to this question is a regretful-sounding but definite “no”. AOC, she believes, is too progressive to build a coalition of voters behind her. The maths just isn’t on her side. That’s before we get to the fact she’s a woman, a young woman and a young woman without children – in a country currently run by a pronatalist administration.

“I’ve always thought the first female president would come out of the Republican Party. news.title: Exclusive: Arkansas Democrat Hallie Shoffner Denies Wanting to Defund ICE After Saying She Would Vote to Defund It

Arkansas Democratic Senate nominee Hallie Shoffner is denying that she wanted to defund Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), despite previously saying she would vote to defund the agency as it currently exists and would not spend another dime on it.

Shoffner, who is challenging Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), made the remarks June 7 at an Immigrant Heritage Month Business Expo in Springdale, Arkansas, as Breitbart News reported.

Asked whether she would vote to defund ICE, Shoffner answered, “I would vote to defund ICE as it exists right now.”

“Immigration and Customs Enforcement was created not that long ago, and it no longer serves the purpose it was originally created for. I would not spend one more dime on ICE, not just because of the human dignity issue, but also the fact that it is now the largest law enforcement agency in the country,” Shoffner said.

She also argued that ICE has “ten times the budget of the organization that fights child sex trafficking” before pointing to hunger in Arkansas as what she described as a more pressing issue.

During the same event, Shoffner described immigrants, regardless of their legal status, as essential to the country.

“I don’t care whether these are folks that have documents or not; this is a community that is essential to the fabric — the social, cultural, and economic fabric — of this country,” she said.

Shoffner accused the government of treating the immigrant community as an enemy and said an immigration system should put “human dignity at the forefront” while considering the needs of small businesses and immigrants themselves.

“What we have to recognize is the folks that are here, whether they have documents or not, are contributing to the small business economy, and the small business economy is what runs America,” she said.

Shoffner also summarized her view of the government’s responsibilities on immigration by saying it should enforce good laws, avoid laws that do not make sense, “treat human beings like human beings,” and “don’t be an asshole.”

As Cotton’s campaign began running attack ads against her, Shoffner commented on the senator’s Facebook page: “Why don’t you roll the full tape, Tom Cotton, and let Arkansans hear what I actually said?”

“I don’t want to defund ICE. I want to reform it,” Shoffner wrote. “But you already know that.”

She then challenged Cotton to a debate, “so Arkansans can hear our positions for themselves.”

Shoffner said on the District 3 Podcast in January that she “grew up in an immigrant community” because farm workers in her area generally came from Mexico and Honduras and that “many of them were undocumented.” She also discussed the use of the H-2A program to recruit workers from Mexico and South Africa, saying her farm employed five Mexican workers who returned annually and arguing that “we must not discount the importance of community — of immigrants who basically power the small business economy.”

news.text:

“I don’t really think it matters. Like, I just really don’t think that it matters. I didn’t have anything to do with it, and I won’t be there,” Shoffner told the Washington Examiner of her deliberate absence from the event.

Shoffner knows the progressive policies she worked her whole life promoting won’t sell in Arkansas, and her campaign reflects that reality. news.title: Markey defies Democrat's age referendum in Massachusetts: 3 takeaways
news.text:
Democrats ignored calls for a generational change in the Massachusetts Senate primary on Sept. 1 between two contenders separated by four decades and a handful of policy differences.

Within 30-minutes of the polls closing in the Bay State, 81-year-old Sen. Ed Markey was the projected winner over 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton, who hung much of his challenge on the need for new blood.

Many primary contests this year have featured veteran incumbents fending off newcomers, who have explicitly argued that many congressional members are too old. The issue remains a raw nerve for Democrats two years after questions about former President Joe Biden's age divided the party.

Markey has served in Congress since 1976 – three years before Moulton was born. He is currently the party's oldest senator and will likely receive another six year term from voters in deep blue Massachusetts.

"Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation," Markey said during a victory speech Tuesday. "It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it’s your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now. Your leadership will show us the way."

At least three other Massachusetts elections saw Democratic primaries drawn along generational lines, with incumbents as old as 77 facing primary foes as young as 27. Chief among them was the battle between Rep. Stephen Lynch, 71, and Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old attorney who served as an aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick.

Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday's election.

Age wasn't nothing but a number

Moulton repeatedly tried to make the Bay State primary contest about the party's aging leadership, which has created a deluge of Gen X, Millennial and Gen Z contenders running in Democratic primaries this year.

"It’s not your age, it's the age of your ideas," Moulton often repeated on the campaign trail.

First elected to the House in 2014, Moulton promised to oppose Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, 75, of New York, if elected and tried to cast Markey as out of touch.

There were moments during the race where that point became clear. During an Aug. 20 debate, Markey struggled say which artificial intelligence platform he uses.

But outside of that fumble Markey crushed questions about his age much in the same way he did six years ago, when he defeated Joe Kennedy III, by showcasing his progressive record and support from a gallery of well-known progressives, such as Rep. Alexandria Oscasio-Cortez, D-New York, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont.

So far in the 2026 primary season at least five congressional Democrats – from Texas to Colorado – who are age 65 or older have lost to younger foes amid the anti-establishment revolt. Now with Markey's win and other outcomes in the Sept. 1 primaries, the Democratic incumbent above retirement age has beaten back the younger challenger in six contests.

Markey eagerly leaned into trans athletes fight

One key difference in the Massachusetts contents compared to other primaries: Moulton, the younger option, was also more moderate compared to Markey on a host of issues.

The senator consistently spotlighted being more progressive and focused his sharpest attacks on Moulton's comments against transgender athletes in 2024.

In the aftermath of Donald Trump's victory, Moulton said he didn’t want his two girls "run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete." The congressman has since said that it was not his intention to hurt people. Markey, unlike most Democrats seeking office this year, leaned into the issue saying his rival had thrown trans kids "under the bus."

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in June that states can ban transgender women and girls from competing on female sports teams, and conservative activists have turned the issue into a wedge most recently with demonstrations at WNBA games.

About 73% of Americans say they are uncomfortable with transgender athletes competing on sports teams that do not match their sex at birth, according to a Pew Research Center poll released in August. That includes 55% of registered Democrats who say the same.

Markey will face Republican John Deaton in the fall in a race rated solidly Democratic.

Hogg throws weight behind younger Massachusetts Democrats

Further down the ballot, there were other contests that pitted Democratic candidates from different generations against each other – attracting attention from national figures.

Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg, who exited the party last year after clashing with leadership over primary endorsements, endorsed attorney Patrick Roath, 39, over Rep. Stephen Lynch, 71, in the state's 8th congressional race, which covers Boston suburbs in the southeastern part of the state.

Hogg's group, Leaders We Deserve, has been supporting many of the younger primary challenges this year including Roath, who received about $470,000 from the group, according to federal campaign finance records.

Similar to Moulton, this campaign centered heavily on age and ideology.

Hogg and his allies, for instance, decried Lynch for accepting corporate PAC money and for being the last House Democrat in office who voted against the Affordable Care Act in 2010.

But that wasn't enough to pull Roath over the edge. Preliminary results showed he lost to Lynch by roughly 15 percentage points, despite attacks that he wasn't progressive enough for a district former Vice President Kamala Harris won with 62 percent of the vote in 2024.

Elder incumbents prevailed in the other primaries that were generational referendums. Rep. Richard Neal, 77, defeated 39-year-old teacher Jeromie Whalen in the 1st Congressional District and Rep. Katherine Clark, 63, the House minority whip, besting Tarik Samman, a 27-year-old union organizer and Jonathan Paz, a 33-year-old immigrant rights organizer, in the 5th Congressional District.

news.title: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch defeats a younger challenger in Massachusetts primary
news.text: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch has defeated a younger, more progressive primary challenger, NBC News projects, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents after a turbulent primary season. Lynch, 71, won renomination over Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. With his win, Lynch staved off an attempt to add him to the list of Democratic officeholders dethroned by rivals pushing for generational change. Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal also secured renomination, defeating teacher Jeromie Whalen in another Democratic primary. On the other side of Massachusetts, Roath outraised Lynch, outspent him significantly on the airwaves and scored The Boston Globe editorial board’s endorsement to go with backing from Patrick, progressive activist David Hogg’s group, Leaders We Deserve, and key teachers unions. That support helped Roath press Lynch for months in one of the toughest fights of his political career. He highlighted Lynch’s various breaks with his party in the past, including votes against the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, for the Laken Riley Act. Roath also called for progressive measures like “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE and restricting military aid to Israel. But Lynch persevered, trumpeting work that he says held the Trump administration accountable and leaning on his decades of experience, including deep relationships with unions and other fixtures in the district. “I got to know this district by living here and regularly attending hundreds of town meetings, not just to speak, but to listen and understand the needs and priorities of the people that I represent,” Lynch said at an August forum sponsored by the League of Women Voters Hingham and others. He touted “tens of billions of dollars that I’ve been able to bring back to our district” and added that he “accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress. You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.” Lynch’s victory means he has avoided the fate of 11 of his House colleagues — including seven Democrats — who lost primary challenges this year as voters took some of their frustrations with Washington out on incumbent lawmakers. Another two senators, both Republicans whose primary opponents got Trump endorsements, also lost primaries this year. Neal also avoided defeat in another primary marked by arguments over generational change and progressive policy proposals. Whalen, 39, a high school teacher, ran a campaign decrying the “old-school political entanglements that got us into this mess” and called to abolish ICE and cut off U.S. military aid to Israel. Neal spent more than $1 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, about 10 times what Whalen spent. Meanwhile, in the open 6th District, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who ran for the Senate but lost that primary to Sen. Ed Markey. Koh was an aide to a variety of top Democrats, including former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, and chief of staff of the U.S. Labor Department, and he was the top fundraiser in the race. Both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris have appeared in an ad for Koh, who has emphasized that he wants to take on Trump and his “corruption,” calling to abolish ICE and pass “Medicare for All.”

news.title: Markey coasts to victory over Moulton in Massachusetts primary
news.text:
Sen. Edward J. Markey, the 80-year-old progressive stalwart from Massachusetts, sailed to victory in his Democratic primary Tuesday as a pair of septuagenarian House Democrats turned back younger challengers. 

With their victories, Reps. Stephen F. Lynch and Richard E. Neal avoided joining the seven House Democrats to lose primary challenges this year, mostly to progressive and younger rivals. 

In the Senate race, Markey was leading Rep. Seth Moulton, whose campaign was built on a call for generational change, 65 percent to 35 percent, with 81 percent of the vote in, according to The Associated Press. 

“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation,’’ Markey told supporters in Boston. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it's your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now. Your leadership will show us the way.”

In deep-blue Massachusetts, Markey will be heavily favored to win in November against Marine Corps veteran John Deaton, who was unopposed for the Republican nomination. Deaton was also the losing GOP nominee to Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren in 2024. 

If he wins, Markey has pledged to serve one last term, at the end of which he would be 86. 

A push for generational change has surged through Democratic politics this year, as the party continues to grapple with the fallout from Joe Biden’s ill-fated 2024 reelection campaign. Among the House Democrats who lost their bids for renomination this year, most were felled by opponents running to their left. 

But in Massachusetts, it was Markey who assumed the progressive mantle against 47-year-old Moulton, highlighting his legislative record and his calls to abolish the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency and pass “Medicare for All.” 

He also embraced transgender rights, criticizing Moulton for saying after the 2024 election that he didn’t want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” (Moulton later apologized.)

Markey relied on support from progressive allies, such as Reps. Ayanna S. Pressley and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, as well as an army of young volunteers.

Moulton made Markey’s age the focus of his campaign, asserting that it was “time for a new generation of leadership to take on a new generation of challenges and opportunities.” At a recent debate, Markey was asked whether he used artificial intelligence. “I use whatever is inside my iPhone or my iPad, whatever comes up,” he responded.

To Moulton, Markey’s halting answer signified the senator’s failure to grasp an essential technology reshaping American society, and it was quickly repurposed for a digital ad.

Moulton’s career has been marked by a willingness to do battle with his party’s elders. In 2014, he won his North Shore congressional seat after dislodging a nine-term Democratic incumbent. A few years later, he led an ultimately unsuccessful uprising against incoming Speaker Nancy Pelosi, then the party’s most powerful woman. And a year after that, he took a stab at running for president; his long-shot bid lasted all of four months.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn't easy, but it is necessary. We started conversations that needed to happen, and I will never stop pushing the Democratic Party and our country to look toward the future,’’ Moulton told supporters in Dorchester. “We didn't achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident that because of this campaign, others will be inspired to buck the system when they're told to wait their turn.”

Markey was first elected to the Massachusetts legislature when Richard M. Nixon served in the White House, then came to the House in 1976 and moved to the Senate after winning a special election in 2013.

This isn’t the first time he has faced a younger Democrat seeking to harness dissatisfaction with the gerontocracy in Washington. In 2020, he was challenged by -Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III. The result was less lopsided: Markey won by about 10 points, handing the Kennedy family its first loss in a Massachusetts election.

House races

In the 8th District, Lynch, 71, staved off challenger Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer and voting rights activist from Jamaica Plain.

With just under 80 percent of votes counted, Lynch was leading Roath 57 percent to 43 percent, the AP reported early Wednesday morning. 

Roath, who had the backing of Leaders We Deserve, a political group founded by Gen Z activist David Hogg, outraised the incumbent during the campaign and criticized his at-times moderate voting record as out of step with the politics of the district. 

But Lynch, a former ironworker from South Boston who was first elected to the House in 2001, focused on his seniority and his working-class background.

In the 1st District in Western Massachusetts, Neal, 77, defeated 39-year-old teacher Jeromie Whalen. But the margin was closer than expected, considering the incumbent's towering fundraising advantage over his challenger. With an estimated 90 percent of votes in, Neal was leading Whalen 54 percent to 46 percent, the AP reported early Wednesday morning. 

Still, the result appears to be the closest primary race of Neal’s near-four-decade congressional career. As the top Democrat on the powerful Ways and Means Committee, Neal emphasized the millions of dollars he’s brought back to the district as he campaigned for a 20th term. He also significantly outraised Whalen, who ran a grassroots campaign from his canary-yellow Toyota cargo van. 

Other House Democrats who easily turned back primary challenges Tuesday included House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, Rep. William Keating and Rep. Jake Auchincloss. 

And in the race to succeed Moulton, former Biden White House adviser Dan Koh beat out a crowd of Democrats vying for 6th District in the state’s North Shore. 

Koh, who also worked for former Labor Secretary and former Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh, was leading the field with 41 percent, just after midnight Wednesday, according to the AP. His nearest challenger, state Rep. Tram Nguyen, lagged more than 10 points behind.

The contest marked Koh’s second run for Congress. He sought the nearby 3rd District seat in 2018, narrowly losing the Democratic nomination to Lori Trahan. In this race, Trahan endorsed Nguyen, while Koh touted endorsements from former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris. He also had the support of former Rep. John F. Tierney, who held the seat before Moulton. 

Koh is favored to prevail over Republican Army veteran Micah Jones in the general election for the deep-blue seat. Victory would make Koh, who is of Korean and Lebanese descent, the first Asian American to represent Massachusetts in Congress.

news.title: Stop the Democrats' Scheme to Pack the Supreme Court
news.text:
Democrats are in a quandary over the Supreme Court. Every four years, they've warned their voters that electing a Republican president will lead to more conservative Supreme Court justices. And yet, since Ronald Reagan's election in 1980 through today, they've lost more presidential elections than they've won. Maybe the voters are telling Democrats something. Maybe Americans don't want the court packed with Sonia Sotomayors who make up or rewrite the laws as they see fit.

So now the Left is angry over the tilt of the court, which has six conservatives and three liberals.

Why? Because elections have consequences. Sorry, this is the price you pay for nominating Michael Dukakis, John Kerry, Hillary Clinton, and Kamala Harris. They aren't exactly hanging around anywhere near the 50-yard line on political ideology.

Now we have Democrats divided on what to do next. Many want Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Elizabeth Warren to be their next presidential nominee. There's no learning curve here.

In the meantime, while Donald Trump is still president, they want urgent action. On the one hand, the democratic socialists want to abolish the highest court of the land. What they want to replace it with is anyone's guess.

Other party leaders want to pack the court with four new liberal justices. Franklin Roosevelt tried this court-packing scheme in 1937, and voters rebelled.

But here they go again. On Sunday, Rep. James Clyburn (SC-06) raised this possibility and disgracefully played the race card when asked about the Supreme Court's recent decisions. He accused Republicans of taking "this country back ... to those rulings of Justice Taney that said, 'No Black man has any right that a white man must respect.'" He was referring to Supreme Court Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the infamous 1857 Dred Scott opinion just before the Civil War.

Does he even know that for 100 years after the Civil War, Democrats were the party of segregation?

What's deeply troubling about this war on the Supreme Court is that this is the institution that is the final check against runaway mob-rule democracy that can trample the rights of the minority. That minority could be blacks, Hispanics, gays, immigrants, or disabled people. They don't seem to understand that pure majority-rule democracy is, as the old saying goes, two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner.

Pure democracy only goes your way until you no longer have 50 percent plus one voters on your side. Clyburn is right that there have been occasions, like the one from 1857 that he mentioned, when the court has made egregiously wrong decisions. But mostly, the court gets it right. It's not clear how stacking the court — on the Left or the Right — could make for more just decisions.

This is why Republicans are so wrong to try to abolish the filibuster in the Senate. We always want to make it HARDER, not easier, to pass new edicts that impair our freedoms.

I, personally, would have no problem expanding the Supreme Court to 12 justices if it could be done in a fair, nonpartisan way. I also strongly support a mandatory retirement age of 75 for all future justices on the court.

But to overly politicize — or, worse, do away with — the Supreme Court and allow Congress to have the last word on the constitutionality of new laws is a dangerous proposition. James Madison once famously described the judiciary as a "bulwark" of our liberties. Hopefully, we will never give up this most important check and balance on runaway government power.

Stephen Moore is a former Trump senior economic adviser and the cofounder of Unleash Prosperity, which advocates for education freedom for all children.

news.title: Markey Wins Key Primary In Victory For Progressives
news.text:
Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey easily won the state’s Democratic primary on Tuesday night, dispatching a younger and more moderate challenger in a significant victory for the party’s progressive wing.

Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton, a decorated veteran of the war in Iraq who had long been tipped as a rising star in the party but struggled to turn his potential into lasting political impact. Moulton, age 47, had made his comparative youth a major part of his campaign against Markey, who has served in Congress for nearly 50 years and will be 86 when his Senate term ends in 2032.

The race was shaping up as a blowout: With about half of the votes counted around 10:30 p.m. Eastern, Markey held a 65% to 35% lead over Moulton. Markey’s margin of victory was likely to easily surpass his performance in 2020, when he defeated former Rep. Joe Kennedy III in another primary centered around age and generational change.

Like in his race against Kennedy, the party’s progressive wing rallied behind Markey, a reliable liberal who has closely aligned with Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and is known for his emphasis on combating climate change. Warren, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) appeared together in a campaign ad for Markey.

While Markey’s victory is a clear win for the left, results elsewhere in Massachusetts did not present a clear narrative. Dan Koh, a former official in President Joe Biden’s administration who ran with the backing of Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, won the primary to replace Moulton in Congress.

Koh, who held senior non-editorial roles at HuffPost more than a decade ago, was considered the moderate option in the primary as progressives rallied behind state Rep. Tram Nguyen.

Two other races between younger progressives and veteran establishment members of the House remained too close to call. 

Recent surveys had shown Markey pulling away from Moulton, who had won his seat in Congress more than a decade ago by successfully defeating Rep. John Tierney in a primary to win a seat representing the Boston suburbs on the state’s North Shore. 

Moulton’s military credentials ― the Boston Globe once famously revealed he had actually underplayed his achievements ― made him a closely watched figure on Capitol Hill. But he made an ill-conceived challenge to then-Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi following the 2018 elections and followed it up with a flop of a presidential campaign in 2020. 

Democratic voters’ anger and desire for generational change following the political failure of an octogenarian president seemingly gave Moulton a fresh opening to do what Kennedy could not six years earlier.

Moulton, however, was a rare candidate to mount a generational change challenge from the party’s center. While not an avowed centrist, Moulton is generally skeptical of the party’s far left and questioned whether Democrats’ stance in support of allowing transgender children to play sports cost the party the 2024 presidential election.

Markey and his allies pounced on those comments, using them to question whether Moulton would reliably stand up for progressive principles, and Moulton ultimately apologized for them.

“I am confident that because of this campaign, others will be inspired to buck the system when they are told to wait their turn,” Moulton said in a speech after he conceded to Markey. 

Markey is set to face Republican John Deaton, an attorney closely associated with the cryptocurrency industry, in November. The race is considered safely Democratic.

news.title: Why MS NOW rates the Texas Senate race a toss-up
news.text:
Since the dust settled on the Texas primaries — including a late May runoff — the Senate race there has looked competitive. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton have been close in the polls, but Texas’ recent electoral history led us to give the GOP the edge for most of the summer, even with Paxton being a weaker nominee than the incumbent he ousted in the primary with President Donald Trump’s help, Sen. John Cornyn.

Now, as Labor Day marks the unofficial start of campaign season, it’s clear that Texas has become a top-tier battleground. A worsening political environment for Republicans, confirmatory polling data and an emerging fundraising picture are impossible to ignore. Texas is truly a toss-up.

The polling

A series of recent polls confirms that vote preferences are evenly divided between Talarico and Paxton now. The two tend to be within a few points of each other in public polls. More often than not, Talarico has a small lead, but within the margin of error.

Skeptics will note that Democrats thought Texas was in reach once before, in 2018, when Beto O’Rourke lost to Sen. Ted Cruz by 3 points. But it’s notable that Talarico is polling better than O’Rourke was at this stage. Moreover, there is a Libertarian Party candidate on the ballot again, which gives disaffected Republicans a non-Democratic option if they can’t stomach voting for Paxton. That also means a candidate could theoretically win without claiming an outright majority.

The polls also suggest a tough issue landscape for Republicans up and down the ballot, with economic concerns displacing the border as the most salient issues for voters. Many Texans simply feel that they can’t get ahead, a sense compounded by high gas and grocery prices. Voters are also clearly concerned about ethics issues, and a majority call Paxton corrupt. A Fox News poll a month ago found more concern that Paxton lacks the character to serve in the Senate than concern about Talarico being too extreme. And another recent poll finds that most voters disapprove of how the state leadership is handling political corruption.

https://www.tiktok.com/@msnow/video/7680772713773829390?_r=1&_t=ZT-99Of3UPdam6

Polls also consistently show an enthusiasm gap, with Democrats likelier to vote this fall than Republicans. Differential turnout — that is, Kamala Harris voters turning out at higher rates than Trump voters — could shift the electorate to the left by a few points, relative to recent elections.

On top of that, Talarico is posting impressive numbers with Latino voters and independents. While Trump carried Texas Latinos by 10 points, according to 2024 exit polls, that margin looks like it has flipped, with Talarico often ahead by about 20 points or more. And while independents split evenly in 2024, Talarico may need to win them by double digits to be victorious.

The primary

Polling data isn’t the only evidence of an enthusiasm gap and a shift among Latinos; the primary had signs of each. For the first time in a midterm cycle since 2002, Democratic primary votes outnumbered Republican ones. The hard-fought Democratic primary campaign clearly generated real interest, and turnout modeling suggests the vast majority of those primary voters will turn out again in the general.

A precinct-by-precinct look at the results shows why that matters. Turnout rose most in Latino precincts. Roughly 3 in 4 Latino voters chose the Democratic primary over the Republican one. All of this helped Talarico, who did better in places with more Latino voters.

A Latino shift was also evident in February’s special election in Texas’s 9th state senate district, which includes much of Fort Worth. The district swung more than 30 points and flipped to Democrats, with heavily Latino parts shifting even more. While primaries and special elections bring out a different electorate than a general election, when these indicators all point in the same direction as the polling, they’re harder to dismiss.

The candidates’ own accounts tell a lopsided story. When it comes to the money each candidate has raised for their own campaign committee, we compare the cash-on-hand numbers from their latest Federal Elections Commission reports. That only gives us the picture through the end of June, which had Paxton with about $1.8 million on hand versus Talarico’s $21.5 million. Talarico has been spending some of that money to get on the air with ads in an expensive state with multiple metropolitan areas and media markets.

But the fact that Talarico has used money to run ads throughout the summer and, according to the Texas Tribune, “is going up with his first negative television ad of the U.S. Senate race” at the beginning of this critical stretch is a clue. Another clue is that while at least one outside group has recently started running ads aimed at boosting Paxton and making Talarico look cozy with foreign interests, no general election ads have dropped directly from Paxton’s campaign. Paxton said in a Fox News interview on Sunday that his own ads are coming.

What Paxton does have on his side are well-funded allies: outside groups like the Trump-affiliated MAGA Inc. super PAC and America PAC, the group connected to Elon Musk. Both should be aligned with Paxton and are sitting on a boatload of cash that could flood the airwaves in Texas. “I know that they are going to be a part of this,” Paxton said of such groups during his Fox News interview. “We can’t coordinate on how much or what. It’s coming.”

If ads from those groups start to drop, that will factor into the future ratings. For now, because Paxton is still waiting for that money, we are factoring this lack of messaging to the voters of Texas into our current analysis.

What else might change

Texas remains a heavily Republican state in terms of its electorate’s baseline partisanship. Talarico’s path to victory depends on his ability to drive up Democratic turnout, decisively win Latinos and independents and, relatedly, persuade some Trump voters to move to the Democrat this time. While the polling suggests that’s all doable, it’s by no means a guarantee.

In fact, there are clues in the current polling data that Paxton has a bit of room to grow in support. Republicans tend to have higher proportions of undecided voters than Democrats do, and as the campaign heats up, partisans typically coalesce behind their nominee. That’s one way the small polling leads Talarico currently enjoys could evaporate.

And Texans by and large still view the Democratic Party less favorably than the GOP. A big question is the extent to which voters will distinguish the Senate candidates from party brands. Negative partisanship is a strong force, and at the end of the day, Republican-leaning voters may decide that Paxton, flawed though he may be, is the lesser of two evils. After all, despite his well-known ethical issues and election denialism, he has managed to win statewide three times already. (That said, his vote share trailed Gov. Greg Abbott’s in 2018 and 2022, and that was before Paxton was impeached for abuse of power by the Texas House of Representatives.)

Texas has remained a solidly red state in the Trump era, and in fact hasn’t elected a Democrat to statewide office in more than 30 years. If we see indications this fall that Paxton is on track to keep that streak alive, we will revisit our race rating. We’ll do the same if Talarico looks in a stronger position to break it.

news.title: California drivers could bankroll Gavin Newsom’s security after he leaves office under $20M budget carveout
news.text:
California drivers could soon be footing the bill for increased security services for current and former state politicians, including term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is eyeing a White House bid.

State lawmakers on Tuesday, the final day of California’s legislative session, approved a budget tweak adding $20 million to the California Highway Patrol to pay for security for current and former state officials and their immediate family members. 

That could include Newsom, whose term ends in January 2027, along with legislators, judges and other constitutional officers. 

The $20 million would come from the Motor Vehicle Account to increase “authorization for security services” by the highway patrol, according to an analysis of a state budget bill. Drivers pay into that account with registration fees.

Another companion bill, also passed this week, touches on the already-existing authority of the highway patrol to provide security for current and former elected officials. That measure would expand that protection to include immediate family members.

The governor’s office told KCRA that the additional funding is needed, though it did not specifically address whether Newsom plans to take advantage of it after leaving office.

“We unfortunately live in a time when threats and political violence against public officials are very real and on the rise,” a Newsom spokesperson said.

“Protecting current and former officials facing credible threats as a result of their public service has long been a bipartisan notion, and these security decisions are based solely on threat assessments by law enforcement.”

The legislation calls on the highway patrol to assess threat levels to an official to determine how long security will be provided, and to re-assess every six months. Threat levels can’t be adjusted until a re-assessment under the bill.

Both measures await Newsom’s signature before becoming law.

However, the security funding has raised skepticism over whether it would make sense to continue paying for Newsom and his family’s security as he travels across the nation to key battleground or early-presidential election states, such as Michigan and South Carolina.

Another Californian and potential presidential contender, former Vice President Kamala Harris, attracted scrutiny for her state taxpayer-funded security while on a post-vice presidency book tour.

“It is in my opinion inappropriate, and it might even be unconstitutional,” state Sen. Roger Niello, a Republican on the senate’s budget committee, told KCRA. 

Niello was referring to law that restricts how motor vehicle account revenues can be used.

“He has a sizable account for his campaign,” Niello added about the governor. “As opposed to the people paying their registration fees paying for that.”

California motorists already face some of the highest registration fees in the nation, averaging around $600, the fifth highest, according to one estimate.

Legislative consultants noted the motor vehicle account, while right now fiscally stable, can face insolvency starting 2028. Now is not the right time to pull $20 million from the fund, Niello said.
news.summary: The money would specifically provide California Highway Patrol officers to serve as the personal security for current or former elected officials and their families.

news.text:
One of the defining narratives of our hellish reality since November 2024 has centered around the Democratic Party’s rank cowardice, and a tsunami of resentment rising from their own voters in response to what they rightly see as ineffectual leadership that isn’t willing to exercise the power it has won for itself. “The Democrats are allergic to power” was surely one of the first sentences I wrote for Paste Politics back when I started by media career in 2016, and it has been true nearly every day since.

It still is true, because sincere actions speak louder than words and we are where we are thanks to a litany of Democratic Party mistakes, but everyone knows that the establishment doesn’t say any words that haven’t first been approved by overpaid consultants talking to focus groups, so the words out of one of the most powerful Democrats alive this weekend were pretty newsworthy in my book.

James Clyburn says on @meetthepress.com that he supports adding four seats to the Supreme Court: “A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court.”
— Sahil Kapur (@sahilkapur.bsky.social) August 30, 2026 at 7:27 AM

In 2007, Rep. Clyburn became the first Black Majority House Whip since the days of Reconstruction, and he helped decide the 2020 presidential election when he and Barack Obama got Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar out of the race and united a front behind Joe Biden in Clyburn’s home state of South Carolina, defeating the two challengers to his left in Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. He was first elected to Congress in 1992, and has seen the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) grow to twice its size from when he joined, and now it is shrinking thanks to John Roberts’ Supreme Court gutting the Civil Rights Act.

In the wake of Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts declaring that racism against Black people is over, and therefore it’s okay to be racist to Black people again, Jim Crow legislators across Republican states have done everything they can to gerrymander Black Democrats out of existence. Bloomberg’s Nia-Malika Henderson spoke to Clyburn back in June, and she wrote that “as many as six CBC members could lose their seats in 2026 as a result of redistricting, though Representative Yvette Clarke, who chairs the group, has said that 19 are vulnerable.”

Inch by inch, this GOP is dedicated to return to the days of the three-fifths compromise behind the rank criminality of the Roberts Court, and one big difference between Clyburn and other powerful establishment Democrats like Chuck Schumer is that the CBC knows an existential threat when it sees one. Upon the CBC’s establishment in 1971, founding member Rep. William L. Clay, Sr. said, “Black people have no permanent friends, no permanent enemies…just permanent interests,” and we are watching Clyburn follow this thesis and push his party to adopt a pretty ambitious political position that would help defend the CBC from the GOP project to destroy it.

Just days before Clyburn made this pitch, Kamala Harris told the National Urban League Conference that “We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts,” and Rep. Jamie Raskin made this same case back in May at a House Judiciary hearing. Thirteen is still too little, but when you’re trying to unmoor a status quo that has existed since 1869, you’re not going to get everything you want up front, and any initial ask to shift the Overton Window should be on the smaller side. This isn’t incrementalism, this is a civic intervention to reverse a century-plus of neglect. We must re-teach the Constitution to a truly braindead Beltway political and media elite who don’t know what the word amendment means, and seem to earnestly believe that a handful of influential 20 somethings having their own posting war a couple centuries ago is all the guidance we need, even though the Founders gave us an amendment explicitly telling us it was not all we need.

Rep. James Clyburn says he supports expanding the Supreme Court: "13 is a pretty good number. A baker's dozen would be a good number to have on the Court."

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar.com) 10:44 AM · Aug 30, 2026

And it’s not just Clyburn and Harris making the kind of specific promise you can readily turn into legislation (in fact, this legislation to add four seats to SCOTUS was proposed by a group of House and Senate Democrats in 2021, and House Majority Leader Nancy Pelosi said she had “no plans” to bring it to the floor for a vote). Current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, also a CBC member, said last month that “dramatic Supreme Court reform is necessary… there’s a variety of different options that are on the table and I think that we can’t foreclose any single one of them.” 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has not gone this far, but he did say in 2024 that “I feel very strongly for the sake of the republic we need reform in the courts” and told NBC in an interview that if they were to win in November, some kind of Supreme Court reform would be “a very big priority” for a Democratic Congress who punted on it in their last majority. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse sits on the Senate Judiciary Committee, and he just introduced an 18-year term-limits bill last month. I think a lot of elected Democrats have realized they royally fucked up not doing this under Biden when they had the chance, and this isn’t just them making the right mouth sounds to placate their base. Real SCOTUS reform has bicameral support, and should 2028 go the way we hope, eventual support in the executive branch too.

Presidential hopefuls like Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro told the New Hope Free Press in July that “I think everything needs to be on the table. I think we need radical reform.” Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker, also a likely 2028 candidate, told The Bulwark that Court expansion “may be what we need.” America’s preeminent political weathervane and the thirstiest 2028 wannabe contender, California Governor Gavin Newsom, has long opposed SCOTUS expansion, yet he finally relented in an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen who was advocating for it, telling the podcaster “I’m with you. I’m done winning arguments, we gotta win.” In that same piece, Cohen plays a clip of Sen. Adam Schiff on CNN saying he agrees that the Court should be expanded. The great lefty hope of 2028, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, told Fox News to their faces that “I do, I think we should be expanding the Court.”

This is a big freaking deal, a seismic shift in the Democratic Party where a cowed establishment has started making FDR-sized promises. These are just words and should be treated as such, but the messaging consistency for something clearly still being tested out is notable. They are obviously talking about this among themselves. The base has made this a non-negotiable item. Republicans have pushed Democrats into a corner with no good options, and the fact that Gavin Newsom backed California’s gerrymandering response to Texas and now capitulated on SCOTUS reform is a literal marker of where the party is on this subject. The moderate Democratic position seems to be 13 Supreme Court seats, not nine. Which is good! But!

The politicians advocating for 13 justices are basically just saying we should follow the parameters of the Judiciary Act of 1869 that tied Supreme Court justices to the number of circuits, which at the time was nine and now is thirteen. Just adding four seats and doing little else is putting lipstick on a pig, and ruining the branding of the 5-4 Pod so they have to change it to 7-6 while they keep the content. It’s a good start to this debate, but it’s not where it should end.

And we shouldn’t stop at just one branch of serious government reform. The Senate exists to block legislation from passing and there’s a reason why the world’s most successful democracies don’t have one, while the House is the size it is thanks to the 1929 Permanent Apportionment Act. Our democratic representation is anchored to the demographics of an entirely different generation. When the Supreme Court was set at nine justices, we only had 37 states. When the House was fixed to its present-day size, we had 48 states while New Mexico and Arizona weren’t old enough to vote and Oklahoma wasn’t old enough to rent a car. If the Supreme Court grew proportionally with the United States population since 1869, it would have around 80 members. If the House also grew proportionally to population since 1929, it would have more than 1,200 seats, not 435.

I’m not saying we should expand the Court proportionally to our population, just demonstrating how we don’t need to be constrained by the logic of a law passed in 18 freaking 69. But we can argue about the details of SCOTUS reform later. For now, we should be happy and relieved to see serious rhetorical movement among Democratic Party power players on a seminal issue that threatens our democracy. I am not one to trust the Democratic Party as many of my most astute haters love to yell at me over, but I have become convinced the Overton Window has truly shifted here. When Clyburn speaks, Democratic Party power players listen, and this has become an issue where the party base and its politicians are clearly aligning. Keep yelling at them for not doing enough, and don’t forget to praise them when they listen–it’s working.
