news.title: House to Vote on Locking Supreme Court at 9 Justices as Democrats Float Expanding It
news.text:
The House is expected to vote this week on a proposed constitutional amendment that would fix the size of the Supreme Court at nine justices. The number of justices is currently set by statute, which Congress can change by simple majority. If ratified, the amendment would place the figure in the Constitution, where changing it would require another amendment.

The measure, H.J. Res. 1, was introduced by Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) and consists of a single sentence: “The Supreme Court of the United States shall be composed of nine justices consisting of one chief justice and eight associate justices.”

Under Article V of the Constitution, a proposed amendment must pass both the House and the Senate by a two-thirds vote before going to the states. The resolution gives states seven years from the date of submission to ratify it, and ratification requires the legislatures of three-fourths of the states—38 of 50.

Some Democrats have been pressing for a larger court. Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) introduced legislation on May 4 to increase the court from nine justices to 13, and other prominent Democrats such as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) have all recently floated a larger court.

Green’s bill has no cosponsors and has not moved out of the Judiciary Committee. Earlier versions of the Judiciary Act, sponsored by Rep. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.) in 2021 and 2023, also proposed a 13-justice court and did not receive a committee vote. The committee report on H.J. Res. 1 cites those bills as the reason for acting, saying a recent set of expansion proposals makes it necessary to fix the number in the Constitution.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) listed the resolution among the week’s floor items in his weekly schedule preview, alongside a separate resolution from Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.) condemning socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America.

“Radical left Democrats and the [Democratic Socialists of America] want to politicize and restructure the Supreme Court, effectively destroying the constitutional safeguards our Founders put in place,” Scalise’s office wrote in the preview. “For years, Democrats have called for packing the Supreme Court with more left-wing judges and now the [Democratic Socialists of America] is going even further by calling to abolish the Supreme Court and replace it with a judicial system subordinate to Congress.”

Biggs said in a June statement after the resolution cleared committee that the court had become a target.

“Our nation’s founders built a system of checks and balances to protect citizens from concentrated power—a central part being the U.S. Supreme Court, whose duty is to defend the rights and freedoms of every American, not to serve as a political tool for any party,” Biggs said. “The judiciary was designed to be the quiet guardian of liberty, insulated from the passions of the moment. Unfortunately, special interests have been increasing their attacks on the Court, threatening to pack this iconic American institution to ensure favorable outcomes for their causes.”

House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) told reporters on Tuesday that he would vote against the resolution and characterized it as a message vote timed to the midterm elections.

“This is such a fake issue that Republicans are putting on,” Aguilar said. “The American public aren’t asking about this. I went around the country, the vice chair did a bunch of travel, I did a bunch of travel. Nowhere, ever, are people saying, ‘You know what we should do? We should cap the number of Supreme Court justices.’”

Aguilar said he expected the resolution to reach the floor on Wednesday and that he would oppose it.

“I understand that Republicans are gonna try to put up votes—socialism vote, Supreme Court justices,” he said. “These are all just kind of show votes. Assuming that this passes a rule, I'll vote no, because this is just a complete show vote.”

Asked whether Democrats who have called for adding seats put the party at odds with its own leadership, Aguilar said expansion is not what the caucus is pushing.

“The argument among folks in our party is we want to reform the court, but we’ve said very clearly that that should be a code of ethics that they actually follow,” he said. “There needs to be real reform within the government side of what we do, and that’s every branch of government. Democrats have been loud and clear about that, and we continue to advocate for that, and we will when we’re in the majority.”

The House Judiciary Committee approved the resolution on June 3 by a vote of 15–8. No Democrat on the committee voted to report the resolution to the floor.

In dissenting views filed with the committee report, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the committee’s ranking Democrat, criticized the vote as being about giving up congressional power rather than the number of justices.

“The question H.J. Res. 1 presents is not really about whether nine should suddenly become a magic number of justices for the Supreme Court,” Raskin wrote. “It’s about whether this Republican-controlled Congress—which has already surrendered congressional war powers, congressional taxing and tariff powers, and congressional spending powers to a president desiring to be a king—should now permanently relinquish another constitutional power that the Framers gave to us in Article I.”

Raskin also accused the Supreme Court of being “profoundly partisan and lopsided” and wrote that the measure is meant to freeze the current court in place, pointing to the handling of two vacancies during President Barack Obama’s and President Donald Trump’s first terms.

He said that the amendment has no realistic path to becoming part of the Constitution.

Congress has changed the court’s size several times, according to a Congressional Research Service report cited by the Judiciary Committee.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 created a six-member court. Congress voted in 1801 to reduce it to five, but that change never took effect—the law applied only once a seat came open, and Congress repealed it before any vacancy occurred.

Several statutes over the following decades changed the number again, reaching 10 justices during the Civil War, the largest the court has ever been. Congress cut the number to seven in 1866, again through attrition rather than removing sitting justices, then set it at nine in 1869. That was the last time Congress changed the court’s size.

The report, “‘Court Packing’: Legislative Control over the Size of the Supreme Court,” says scholars disagree about why Congress made those changes, with some pointing to practical needs such as caseload and others arguing they were driven by political considerations.

The committee report says that during the period when the court’s size moved with the number of circuits, justices were also responsible for hearing cases in the lower federal courts, and that once that practice ended, there was no longer a reason to change the court’s size as new lower courts were created.
news.summary: Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) said the amendment would insulate the court from political pressure, while Democrats criticized it as a show vote.
news.author: Chase Smith

news.title: Silicon Valley fascism is waging war on democracy
news.text:
"Billionaires have become radicalised against democracy," the American independent journalist Gil Durán tells the ABC.

"We have to realise how much power we have, and to stop being tuned out from the very real threat we face from a billionaire class that has gone off the edge of sanity into an altered reality.

"But we also need to realise where we're at, how we got here, and who's paying for it all.

"It's not just Trump anymore. It's a regime. And it's a regime that is funded and supported and strengthened by the oligarchs of Silicon Valley."

That is Mr Durán's warning to Australians.

He was speaking to the ABC about his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy.

It describes how tech billionaires and venture capitalists in the US have cultivated a virulently anti-democratic ideology for decades and how they're using technology to remake today's world, with consequences for everybody.

And it is resonating with American readers, debuting as an instant New York Times bestseller after its release on August 18.

"America has been revealed as highly vulnerable to destruction," the book explains.

"Pushing it to the brink wasn't particularly difficult. It required only enough wealthy and influential people who were willing to fund it, or at least go along with it quietly.

"Democracy's enemies specialise in long-term strategies, and they have enough money to operate in perpetuity; they are scheming for global control," it warns.

Replace democracy with corporate dictatorship

We're all short of time.

We appreciate books that help us quickly understand the ideas driving contemporary politics and the technological future of countries like the United States and Australia.

And this book is one of them.

It tells the story of how anti-democratic, anti-government, and aggressively anti-tax ideas were fused and incubated in Silicon Valley in the 1980s and 1990s, and how strange books like 'The Sovereign Individual' (1999) inspired a generation of new tech entrepreneurs to build the technology to start undermining national governments and their currencies.

It reveals how decades ago, influential figures in Silicon Valley began describing democracy as a flawed operating system that had to be replaced by a corporate dictatorship.

It explains how, back in 1999, Peter Thiel (the co-founder of PayPal and Palantir) was predicting that official Washington D.C. would be too dumb to understand the encryption technology that was emerging out of Silicon Valley at the dawn of the millennium, and that "incredible technological forces" were pushing the world in the direction of digital currency and limited government.

It records how some female journalists, like Paulina Borsook, sounded the alarm early about the toxic culture emerging from Silicon Valley's chatrooms in the 1990s, but the mainstream U.S. tech press dismissed and ridiculed them.

Borsook's book Cyberselfish (2000), which fell out of print, is now being called "prophetic" and is being republished this month, after 26 years.

And it details how Silicon Valley billionaires want to carve up the world into thousands of tax-free "economic zones" and create their own sovereign jurisdictions.

Foreign Correspondent's recent story on Próspera, the "libertarian utopia" on a Caribbean island off the coast of Honduras, is part of the same story of Silicon Valley's yearning to "exit" the world we live in.

A philosophy of 'exit'

Ultimately, Durán's book describes how a lot of the behaviour and investment decisions of Silicon Valley's influential venture capitalists in recent decades can be explained by their philosophy of "exit".

That is, it explains how they want to "exit" (i.e. abandon) democracy, with its laws and regulations and fiat currencies, and create new forms of government and new jurisdictions (in space, the ocean, on land, and in the cyber world) that use digital currencies.

"It doesn't make sense for these billionaires, the most successful and wealthy people in our society … to be investing in this massive disruption like this unless they are zealots who believe it's time to completely collapse the world order," Durán told the ABC.

"In my book, I tell the story of this idea, that that's exactly what they see as necessary and inevitable."

And the same names keep popping up in the book.

Names like Peter Thiel, Curtis Yarvin, Elon Musk, Marc Andreessen, Mark Zuckerberg, Balaji Srinivasan, Sam Altman, and JD Vance, among others, many of whom spent years in Silicon Valley's cauldron.

They would create culturally potent companies like PayPal, Palantir, LinkedIn, Tesla, Uber, Lyft, Airbnb, Facebook, Instagram, and Amazon, and technologies like Bitcoin and Coinbase.

"In 2025, the tech industry revealed its true face," Durán writes.

"Devoid of any moral scruples or loyalty to democratic principles, many of Silicon Valley's most well-known figures chose to openly ally themselves with a president who would soon, with their help, check every box in the authoritarian playbook.

"Instead of filing lawsuits against the administration, tech giants lavished him with money and support.

"As his administration carried out a shock-and-awe effort to destroy the pillars of American democracy, the most powerful and prominent figures in tech stood behind him," he writes.

An open enemy of democracy

Durán writes simply and clearly.

He is a former opinion editor for The Sacramento Bee and editorial page editor for The San Francisco Examiner.

He is an independent journalist who runs The Nerd Reich, a newsletter about "tech authoritarianism, billionaire extremism, the Network State and the meta politics of California."

Politically, he used to work as a press secretary for California's Democratic governor Jerry Brown and he served as Kamala Harris's communications director when she was California attorney general.

But he does not hold back criticism of US Democrats.

"Democratic leaders continue to operate as if the tech sector has not become an open enemy of democracy itself," he writes in the book.

"They speak of AI and billionaires and crypto in flattering and friendly terms, no doubt hoping to remain beneficiaries of campaign checks from tech billionaires.

"While the champions of tech fascism see the Republican Party as the best vehicle for its hopes, they also understand the inherent corruptibility of the Democratic Party, which also serves its wealthy donors more than it serves anyone else."

We can have billionaires or democracy

The final chapter of his book is a call to arms.

"We can have billionaires, or we can have democracy. We cannot have both," he writes.

And he tells the ABC that the growing backlash in the United States against data centres and AI shows people do not like the future tech billionaires have been forcing on everyone.

He said normally in US politics new technology would be promoted in terms of how many jobs it would create, not destroy, but that wasn't the story that these tech companies had been telling investors.

"The oligarchs of Silicon Valley have done their best to terrify everybody, and so what's happening right now is absolutely logical and rational and reasonable," he said."The data centres are viewed, I think, as a physical manifestation of billionaire power on the land that's become this bogeyman, this monster, this alien invasion that arrives in your community to suck up your water and pollute your air and eat up your land, all for the promise that it will fuel a technology that will kill your job and possibly wipe humanity off the face of the planet. "What's not to love?" he jokes grimly.

And he said data centre protests in the US have become a focal point for regular people, from all walks of life, to come together as a community to fight billionaire power and learn what was happening in neighbouring counties.

"The billionaire city in Solano County, for instance, Republicans are even more opposed to it than Democrats are," he said.

"Similarly for crypto. Some of Trump's most fervent supporters got completely robbed by putting money into these crypto schemes, so on a very personal level they know that this is bad.

"We're seeing movements like "Purge Palantir," to get Palantir out of our government, our cities, our hospitals and stores.

"And then there's "DeFlock", which is pushing back against "Flock" cameras [automated licence plate readers] and the new surveillance state where everything will somehow be safe and secure by all of us being under surveillance.

"People are waking up."
news.summary: The author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, has a warning.
news.author: Gareth Hutchens

news.title: Hunter Biden Slams Kamala As a 'Not Very Good Politician'
news.text:
Hunter Biden had some rather interesting things to say about former Vice President Kamala Harris as speculation about a potential 2028 presidential run persists.

During an interview with podcaster Mehdi Hasan, Biden said Harris was not as loyal to former President Joe Biden as some might think.

Hasan brought up past comments Biden made suggesting that Harris is “not a very good politician” and pointed out that she “was given only 107 days by your dad to try and win an election.”

“And $2 billion,” Biden said. 

Hasan also pointed out that during her debate against President Donald Trump, she accepted the notion that there was no daylight between her and the elder Biden. The host argued that this “cost her the presidency” because she “stayed loyal” to the former president. 

“And many would say, here you are throwing her under the bus, saying she's not a very good politician,” Hasan concluded.

“Here's what I'd also like to say about the vice president,” Hunter replied. “I think that the vice president served the country incredibly well and that she has a deep …rich future in politics. Whether she wants to run for president again, she'll be one of the— if not the front-runner. But she's not a very good politician either.”

When Hasan pressed for details, Biden suggested she could have adjusted her messaging to stand out on her own while touting the supposed accomplishments of the Biden administration.

“She can make daylight between herself and my dad, but not in terms of what they were able to accomplish over that four-year period,” he said. “I think that there might be daylight as issues related to Gaza and as it relates to Israel, that of course she needs to be able to stake her own ground on that.”

Biden later questioned Harris’ loyalty to his father. “So I think people go like, ‘well, she was so loyal to your dad and she didn't do this and that and the other thing.’ Well, maybe from your perspective, but maybe not from mine,” he said.

But Hunter wasn’t keen on giving details. When Hasan asked how Harris was not loyal to the former president, Hunter replied, “That’s between me and her.”

Hasan continued pressing the matter. Hunter replied, “Let me just state it exactly clearly. I think that she was loyal to my father, and I don't think that she was loyal to a fault, however.”

The response from Democrats to the notion that Harris might run again in 2028 has been mixed. She often polls as a frontrunner among Democrat voters. But critics insist that the party needs new leadership and for younger generations to take up the mantle. They also point out that her 2024 loss might be a political narrative that is too difficult to overcome.

news.title: Laura Loomer Is A Mediocre White Woman, And That’s Why She Hates Accomplished Black Women [Op-Ed]
news.text:
Here’s the thing: Laura Loomer is what happens when white mediocrity gets deeply insecure about itself. There’s a reason why every time she calls a Black woman a “ghetto Black bitch” or something similar, she’s always talking about some of the most accomplished Black women in politics or media. 

Loomer called Rep. Jasmine Crockett a “ghetto Black b*tch.” She called Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee a “ghetto b*tch” immediately after the late congresswoman died from pancreatic cancer. She called former Vice President Kamala Harris, New York AG Letitia James, and Fulton County DA Fani Willis “meritless DEI Shaniquas,” simply because they are Black women with more extensive professional and educational resumes than this two–time failure of a politician could ever hope to achieve.

So, now Loomer, the perpetual loser, is going after Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, who is currently a Florida U.S. Senate candidate. In a series of tweets, Loomer called Nixon a “ghetto Black communist b—h,” among other derogatory, anti-Black idioms. She also made multiple references to Nixon speaking “Ebonics,” which, much like with Crockett, seems to be based solely on her being a Black woman who sounds like a Black woman when she speaks, no matter how conventionally articulate she is.

Here’s what Nixon sounds like.

I’m not sure what motivated Loomer to start in on Nixon. According to Newsweek, Loomer took great offense to Nixon’s speech against resolutions honoring conservative activist Charlie Kirk, which makes sense considering Kirk, a community college dropout, was also a loud and proud racist who aimed his mediocre white vitriol at the most prominent, accomplished, and educated Black women in the country, accusing them of being products of DEI. They’re simply two peas in a white supremacist pod for the least supreme of the whites.

So, why did Loomer start in on Nixon? Because Nixon is yet another Black woman who is just plain better than her in every conceivable way.

I mean, come on, y’all — this is nothing more than a temper tantrum thrown by a salty, contemptuous Caucasian who is hiding the shame of her lack of accomplishments behind a facade of loud and proud bigotry. Loomer has clearly decided that since she has failed at everything else, she might as well be successful at being outwardly and unapologetically racist while taking all the backlash on her excess Botox dumpster she calls a chin.

Sorry, but Loomer tosses around way too many personal insults at Black women to be someone who looks like this:

Loomer fancies herself as a right-wing influencer, but what does she influence besides what has to be a world record for physical Jigsaw comparisons?

Anyway, back to the bug Loomer has up her ass for Nixon for whatever reason. Here she is doubling down on her allegations that Nixon is “ghetto,” a “communist,” citing the congresswoman’s protest against racist gerrymandering on the state House floor.

“Do you not think this is ghetto?” asked Loomer, who is apparently forgetting about that time she handcuffed herself to the New York City headquarters of the platform formerly known as Twitter for two hours because she got banned from the platform over her Islamophobic remarks about yet another Black woman, Rep. Ilhan Omar.

I mean, do you not think this is ghetto?

And again, these white supremacist she-Klanigans only inspire more Jigsaw comparisons — on her own posts, no less.

Again, Laura Loomer’s existence isn’t important. She’s a feckless loser who has made racism for the purpose of clout-chasing her entire personality. The real question is why it’s so hard for prominent Republicans to disavow her the way they expect Democrats to disavow any leftist they consider too radical.

And they simply don’t have an answer for that.

Loomer has served as an unofficial adviser to President Donald Trump, who, to be fair, wouldn’t have much room to talk if he were to condemn her public expressions of racism and bigotry. Of course, even if the president had standing to condemn racism, it would be pretty difficult to do so since he has reposted her social media posts as recently as earlier this year.

MAGA and the Republican Party have a clear and consistent white supremacy problem, and Loomer is only a symptom of that. She deserves the same amount of our energy that we would give to something we scraped off the bottom of our shoes. But for MAGA, she’s the ugliest of ugly reflections, and that’s not going to change when someone else is in the White House.

news.title: Democrats Markey, Moulton seek primary win in Massachusetts
news.text:
Sept. 1 (UPI) -- Voters in Massachusetts are heading to the polls Tuesday to vote in the 2026 primary elections, deciding between Democrats Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton as a candidate for the Senate seat.

Markey, 80, is a two-term senator who first entered Congress in 1976 and was elected to the Senate in 2013. He's been a champion of progressive causes and has been endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

Moulton, 47, is a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who was elected to the House of Representatives in 2014. He ran a brief campaign for president in 2020 and has been active in recruiting and training Democratic candidates through the Serve America organization.

The winner will face Republican John Deaton in November. Massachusetts tends to vote heavily Democratic.

In other races, incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, 71 -- the last remaining House Democrat to vote against the Affordable Care Act -- is facing challenger Patrick Routh in the 8th Congressional District of the House.

Lynch, a moderate who has been in office for 25 years, has described himself as "pro-life" and has voted in favor of some of President Donald Trump's immigration policies.

Routh, 39, a Boston attorney, is a more progressive candidate whose campaign has spent more than $1 million in the race against Lynch.

Six Democrats are running for Moulton's 6th Congressional District seat in the House: Bethany Andres-Beck, John Beccia, Jamie Belsito, Dan Koh, Mariah Lancaster and Tram Nguyen.

Koh, a former White House aide for former President Joe Biden, has been endorsed by Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and five Biden Cabinet secretaries. Nguyen, considered to be his main competitor, is a state legislator who is appealing to progressive voters and has endorsements from Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan.

Republican candidates Mike Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve are competing in the Republican primary for governor. Minogue has been endorsed by the party. The winner will face incumbent Democrat Gov. Maura Healey.
news.summary: Massachusetts voters head to the polls Tuesday for primaries, deciding between Democrats Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton for a Senate seat.

news.title: Red state heartlands put a ring on young love while progressive blue cities lag on early marriage
news.text: Young people looking to tie the knot in their twenties may want to rethink where they live. Moving to big coastal cities like New York and Los Angeles could mean lowering the odds of getting married— and living in an area with a high concentration of singles may not lead to more marriages. According to a new study from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS), early-marriage rates are lower in many urban hubs and higher in parts of the heartland. The findings point to a geographical divide in family formation, with young adults in places like Tennessee, Indiana and Utah marrying at higher rates than their coastal big-city peers. "For singles, your best odds of finding love and getting married aren’t in big coastal cities where most singles live, but in middle America, where more marriage‑minded singles are," Wendy Wang, senior researcher at the Institute for Family Studies, told Fox News Digital. THE STATES REVEALED AS BEST TO START A FAMILY AMID CRATERING BELIEF IN THE AMERICAN DREAM The research is part of the IFS’s "Get Married Maps," which provides young people with information about regional marriage trends and examines factors associated with marriage rates. Those factors include employment, religion and recent presidential election results, among others. "Given the many benefits of marriage, a city where more young people are tying the knot might ultimately provide a more fulfilling life than one with just excellent entertainment and tasty food—but few weddings," the study explains. For adults ages 22-29, regions with the highest marriage rates include Provo, Utah, as well as parts of Tennessee, Indiana, Nebraska, Kentucky, Idaho, North Carolina, Kansas and Georgia. In contrast, eight of the ten regions with the lowest early-marriage rates are concentrated in the New York and Los Angeles metropolitan areas. NORTH TEXAS DOMINATES IN POPULATION GROWTH AS BIG BLUE CITIES FAIL TO RECOVER TO PRE-PANDEMIC LEVELS "These findings demonstrate that, for young adults, the ‘best place’ to get married may depend largely on when they hope to marry. Those who are committed to marrying in their twenties may want to think carefully about moving to a major coastal city; meanwhile, those same cities could be an excellent option—though not the only choice—for marriage-minded adults in their thirties," the study notes. While coastal cities have lower marriage rates for 20-somethings, the picture changes for singles in their thirties. For adults ages 30 to 39, regions with the highest marriage rates include portions of the New York, San Jose, Los Angeles and Chicago metropolitan areas, along with suburbs in Texas and Indiana. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' Wang also explained that the research shows living in an area with a large population of single young people may not improve the odds of finding a future spouse. "If you think your best chance of finding someone to marry is in the places with the most singles, think again," Wang told Fox News Digital. "The nation’s top 10 areas with the highest share of singles (more than 80 percent unmarried) are far from the places where most new marriages are happening." The IFS research found that areas with more single men relative to single women tend to have higher female marriage rates, but the relationship is even stronger when researchers measure the ratio of full-time-employed single men to all single women. Military-adjacent regions like Oceanside, California, and Fayetteville, North Carolina, as well as tech-heavy areas such as Mountain View and Sunnyvale, California, have some of the highest ratios of full-time-employed single men to single women. DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES However, the link between male income and marriage rates varies by age. For women in their thirties, regions with a higher ratio of single men earning at least $60,000 a year had higher marriage rates. That financial link disappears for women in their twenties, suggesting younger couples place less emphasis on high salaries when deciding to tie the knot. Still, on an individual level, young men in their twenties who earn $60,000 or more are about twice as likely to marry as lower earners. "Single men’s jobs remain one of the strongest factors driving marriage in America," Wang added. Regional marriage rates for young adults in their twenties also showed a strong positive correlation with areas that backed Donald Trump over Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. However, for adults in their thirties, this correlation flips and turns negative. "One possible explanation is that more rural parts of the country, where Trump generally performed better than Harris, often have higher marriage rates for adults in their twenties," the study notes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The researchers noted that their findings show broad regional patterns, not proof that a particular location or political environment causes people to marry. The study measures where respondents currently live, not necessarily where they met their spouses or lived when they got married. The researchers also acknowledged that some people may have moved after marrying, potentially affecting the marriage rates of certain regions.
news.summary: IFS research reveals young adults in their 20s marry at far higher rates in middle America than in New York or Los Angeles metro areas.

news.title: Obama called Stephen A Smith after he criticized Biden, commentator reveals
news.text:
ESPN commentator and podcaster Steven A Smith has revealed that former president Barack Obama called him prior to the 2024 presidential election after he had criticized Joe Biden to discuss the extent of his influence.

Smith called for Biden to suspend his campaign on his self-titled show in July 2024, shortly before the Democrat did so to make way for his deputy Kamala Harris, observing that he “seems to have lost the step.”

The pundit expressed concern over the elderly president’s cognitive decline after reviewing his recent public appearances, including his disastrous TV debate with Donald Trump.

“Watching him walk, talk, speak, articulate himself, watching him drift and fade, mumble and stumble... Can you do this for four more years?” he asked. 

Smith later expressed regret over his subsequent vote for Harris and criticized Biden for pardoning his son Hunter after he was convicted of three federal gun charges and later pled guilty to tax charges. 

Speaking to The Culture Table about the reaction his comments provoked, Smith told hosts Tori Cooper, Sumatra Abernathy and Ashley Christopher about Obama’s intervention for the first time.

“What I never told y’all, and I never brought up, is that Barack Obama called me too,” he said. “The content of that conversation will remain private because I will not violate trust. He called before the election to discuss my impact, but he didn’t come on the podcast either.

“It was after I said that we need a new president because Joe Biden clearly was done. You know, he clearly looked done. So the point is, folks like to talk to me privately, but then when I ask them to come on camera and to have a fruitful discussion, now they go elsewhere.”

He continued: “So it’s like I’m taking these hits, and these are people that want to facilitate or assist in the facilitation of these narratives being disseminated and projected about me. 

“But the same people calling me privately, having discussions upon which I have never violated. This is the first time anyone has ever heard me publicly state that Barack Obama called me.”

Smith – who has previously attacked Obama’s wife, former first lady Michelle Obama – went on to name other prominent Democrats who have so far declined to guest on his podcast, including Harris, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett.

Asked why they were reluctant, he answered: “I think the Democrats fear my footsteps. I think they know that they have a legitimate fear that I can influence the election potentially.”

Smith was given a “Thumbs Down” award by the National Association of Black Journalists at its annual convention in August, which is handed out to members of the media it feels have not made a helpful contribution to the national debate.

He reacted angrily to the NABJ on social media and told the Culture Table hosts: “The reality is that it was a personal hit job. We can sit up there and lollygag around and act like we don’t know any better. 

“It was a personal hit job. Which, by the way, usually doesn’t phase me. I know you think something phases me, just because you see me commenting on it. No, I'm in this business. I have a platform. I can comment about anything I want to, and I will continue to do so.

“That’s not what this is. This is different. This is a journalism organization that didn’t engage in journalism when it came to critiquing me.”

Smith has hinted at a future presidential run himself but has a long history of personal feuds with everyone from comedian Kevin Hart and former MS NOW anchor Joy Reid to legendary NBA star LeBron James. 

President Trump has also shared his opinions on Smith, calling him “dumb as a rock,” an “arrogant fool” and a “loudmouth huckster” on Truth Social earlier this summer.
news.summary: Outspoken pundit claims former president spoke to him during 2024 presidential election to discuss his influence

William DeFoor, 26, pleaded guilty to causing willful injury or depredation and carrying out physical violence against government officials during a Tuesday court hearing.

“Acts of violence directed against our political leaders, their families, or property, have no place in our society and will not be tolerated,” US attorney Dominick Gerace II said about the guilty plea.

“Our elected leaders, at all levels of government, must be permitted to carry out their duties free from threats, vandalism, and other forms of violence,” Gerace added. “Perpetrators like DeFoor, who put that freedom at risk, particularly through violent, destructive actions, will, like here, be vigorously prosecuted.”

DeFoor’s father, named William, is a successful Harvard University graduate, a pediatric urologist in Cincinnati and professor at the University of Cincinnati’s College of Medicine.

The elder DeFoor donated thousands to Kamala Harris’ failed presidential campaign in 2024 and lives in a $1.3 million house in the tony Hyde Park neighborhood. 

His mother, Catherine, stressed that DeFoor suffered from mental illness. 

“Mental illness is a terrible thing. It is a struggle which can take over the life of a beautiful person,” she said in a statement. “Unfortunately, for our child, it has taken over his life in a way that we never could have imagined.”

In the wee night hours on Jan. 5, DeFoor was caught by Secret Service agents breaching the property line at Vance’s residence and smashing the window of an unmarked law enforcement vehicle, according to prosecutors.

Authorities told DeFoor to drop his hammer and stop, but he ignored them and instead began busting “historic glass windows” on Vance’s property, per the feds. 

Ultimately, he attempted to flee on foot but was nabbed by the Secret Service. 

The damage done to the windows totaled an estimated $28,000, according to the Justice Department. 

The Vances were not at the house at the time of the attack. After President Trump’s victory in 2024, the Vances moved into the vice president’s official residence at the Naval Observatory in DC, which is about 2.5 miles away from the White House.

DeFoor has a rap sheet, which includes a two-year mandatory health treatment sentence for vandalism at an interior design company. 

He was also hit with charges for trespassing at the UC Health psychiatric and emergency services. 

A judge in that case found he wasn’t mentally competent to stand trial. 

The Post reached out to Vance’s office for comment.

news.title: Olivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the same | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Donald Trump, the 80-year-old president of the United States, spent his weekend whining about a lake and posting memes of Donald’s Ducks. While he was busy with his ducks, Olivia Rodrigo, a 23-year-old pop star, spent her weekend trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again. On Saturday, Rodrigo hosted the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival, bringing together female artists to raise money for women-focused non-profits which have had their funding slashed by the Trump administration. The festival raised $10m (£7.4m) which Melinda French Gates matched, bringing the total to $20m.

In a perfect world a singer holding a benefit concert for feminist charities wouldn’t be radical stuff. But we don’t live in a perfect world, do we? We live in hell. Trump has successfully bullied US institutions into doing his bidding. Universities have defunded diversity, equity and inclusion programmes, many media outlets have kowtowed to the US’s self-styled king and tech CEOs have jumped into bed with him. Women’s rights are going backwards globally and our civil liberties are under attack.

It has become depressingly clear just how many of the rich and powerful are self-serving cowards who will abandon social justice issues as soon as it becomes mildly inconvenient. So it was refreshing to see a young musician rally people together in service of reproductive justice at a festival that was proudly feminist and didn’t pretend to be non-political.

Rodrigo has always used her platform to speak out: she’s never been one of those annoying celebrities who insist that remaining apolitical is some sort of noble act. When Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022, the then 19-year-old musician condemned the decision on stage at Glastonbury. Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, also publicly told the Trump administration not to use her music in their “racist, hateful propaganda” when one of her songs was featured in a government video telling undocumented immigrants to self-deport.

Rodrigo has also not been silent about Gaza: a subject many celebrities are terrified to mention, because empathising with Palestinians is a tried-and-tested way to ruin your career. Last year she wrote on Instagram about how “mothers, fathers and children in Gaza are starving, dehydrated and being denied access to basic medical care ...” Rodrigo also gave a nod to Palestine (which, thanks to Israel’s attacks on maternity wards and healthcare is a reproductive justice issue) at a press conference for her Daisy Chain Fields festival, where she wore a dress made by Palestinian fashion brand Nöl Collective.

Speaking on the New York Times’s Popcast earlier this year, Rodrigo said acknowledging social issues is part of expressing herself. “I think it would just be disingenuous to be like, I don’t feel heartbroken about what’s going on in Gaza. As an artist, I feel like that’s just what you do. And that’s my job,” she said.

Frankly, I think it’s the job of everyone with any sort of platform or power. Celebrities shouldn’t have to get political, some will say. No, of course not. But if you have a huge platform and oodles of money and even just a smidgen of a conscience, then you should probably want to use your resources and reach for good, shouldn’t you? Giving money to charity is one thing, but it takes more courage to show people where you stand, knowing there may be repercussions for it. I hate this idea of not “taking sides”: the world is not a football match; political parties are not “teams”. It is not divisive to stand with vulnerable people.

Taylor Swift, the richest female musician in history, certainly seemed to agree with that at one point. She famously stayed quiet in the lead-up to the 2016 election, but later, when more celebrities were doing so, came out to endorse progressive causes. “I need to be on the right side of history,” she said in the 2020 documentary Miss Americana.

But while Swift did endorse Kamala Harris in 2024, she has been very careful about what she says during Trump 2.0. Unlike all the musicians who have publicly condemned the Trump administration for using their music in offensive posts, she seemingly ignored the use of her songs by Trump for months. In recent weeks her songs have been quietly removed from Trump’s ragebait posts, but Swift has not issued any sort of public statement about it. And she certainly hasn’t said anything about issues such as Gaza or ICE.

There are limits to celebrity activism, sure. But in a world where free speech is under attack, it feels increasingly important for celebrities to speak out. Let’s hope Rodrigo’s festival prompts more of her peers to have some guts.

news.title: Three-Time Trump Voter Fumes on Social Media That She Was 'Duped' by a 'Glorified Snake Oil Salesman'
news.text: A self-described three-time Donald Trump voter has publicly turned on the US president, saying on social media this week that she feels she was 'duped' after years of supporting him.Lucy Riles, who described herself as a lifelong Republican, said she had voted for Trump three times and spent what she called an 'embarrassing amount of money' on merchandise and trips to political rallies. In a widely shared post on X, she accused the president of repeatedly disappointing supporters who had remained loyal to him.Her comments come as some Republican voters continue to express frustration over living costs, US involvement in the war with Iran and other administration priorities. Recent polling has also pointed to dissatisfaction within parts of Trump's coalition, although individual voter accounts alone do not establish a wider political break.Trump Supporter Says She Was 'Duped'Riles said the previous 14 months had amounted to 'betrayal after betrayal' and acknowledged that accepting she may have made the wrong political choice had been difficult.She nevertheless stressed that her regret over supporting Trump did not mean she believed former Vice President Kamala Harris would have been a better choice in the 2024 presidential election.Instead, Riles directed her criticism at Trump, calling him a 'glorified snake oil salesman' and arguing that elected leaders should not be placed beyond scrutiny by their supporters.'He is not God nor should he be worshipped as one,' she wrote.Riles said voters should hold politicians accountable even after investing heavily in a political movement or damaging personal relationships because of political disagreements.Her post also criticised several issues that have caused friction among sections of Trump's supporters.Riles objected to the administration's handling of the conflict with Iran and criticised what she characterised as Trump's approach to records linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.She also took issue with Trump's recent defence of data-centre development. The president said this week that communities rejecting large data-centre projects risked becoming 'backwards and poor,' remarks that have generated opposition from some residents concerned about electricity demand, water use and infrastructure.Riles characterised the position as effectively requiring communities to accept such projects regardless of local concerns.She also compared her continued political loyalty to remaining in what she described metaphorically as an emotionally abusive relationship.'I've never been in an emotionally abusive relationship,' Riles wrote, adding that she was not prepared to accept what she viewed as a similar dynamic in politics.Other Trump Voters Voice Economic FrustrationRiles is not the only Trump voter to have publicly voiced dissatisfaction in recent weeks.During an MS NOW coverage from the Iowa State Fair in August, Shane Foot, who also identified himself as a three-time Trump voter, said he was disappointed that everyday costs remained high.Foot complained that prices had not fallen in the way he expected after Trump returned to office.'I'm just over the Trump thing,' he said during the interview.His concerns came as US consumers continued to face higher prices than a year earlier. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures showed consumer prices were 3.4% higher in July 2026 compared with July 2025.Another woman interviewed during the same Iowa coverage described difficulty managing household expenses, particularly groceries and fuel.The cleaning worker said she sometimes spent about $80 (£58.65) on petrol within three days because of her commute. She also discussed the pressure of paying for everyday essentials such as eggs and milk.'It's just hard to feel good when everything's going downhill,' she said.The woman's account reflects her personal financial circumstances rather than the experience of all US voters, but affordability remains a significant political issue for the administration.Marjorie Taylor Greene Backs Voters' Right To Criticise TrumpFormer Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene later amplified Riles's post and defended supporters who criticise Trump when they believe he has failed to keep his promises.'I hear this from people literally every single day,' Greene wrote.She argued that voters should be able to demand accountability from elected officials without being accused of disloyalty.Greene went further, saying that in her view 'the disloyalty comes from Trump, not people like this.'Her comments come after a much broader public falling-out with Trump that preceded her resignation from Congress in January 2026, meaning her latest criticism represents a continuation of an existing political split rather than a sudden change in allegiance.Riles's post and the voter interviews do not prove that Trump's Republican base is undergoing a widespread revolt. However, they add to evidence of dissatisfaction among some supporters over affordability, foreign policy and the direction of the administration.Whether that frustration translates into a lasting shift in voter behaviour remains unclear.

news.title: 'Everyone in Nashville is terrified to say it out loud': Grammy-winning snitch spares no one in savage name-and-shame ranking of singers vying for Dolly Parton's crown as the next Queen of Country: ROB SHUTER
news.text:
Dolly Parton wasn't merely the Queen of Country Music. The title was too small for her five-foot frame.

She could stand at the Grand Ole Opry, then walk onto a Hollywood soundstage beside actresses Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. She wrote her own songs, starred in movies, built businesses, gave away millions of books, launched a theme park and wore wigs taller than some careers.

Parton was something rarer than a superstar: a celebrity whom everybody loved. In America. Imagine.

That's the real legacy left behind by the Smoke Mountain Songbird after her death last week at 80 years old. 

But can anyone really replace Dolly?

Music industry sources tell me that the knives are out in Nashville as the entourages of established stars jostle with posses of the up-and-comers.

Shania Twain broke down country's walls. Carrie Underwood has the voice. Miranda Lambert has credibility. Ella Langley has the momentum. But those in the know agree they can't hold a candle to Parton.

One obvious answer is Taylor Swift.

She began as a teenage Nashville songwriter. Country became country-pop, then pop, then stadium culture. Much like Parton, Swift stopped belonging to a genre long ago.

On paper, Swift has everything it takes to fill Parton's boots: country roots, songwriting credibility, business instincts, crossover appeal and global fame.

'Taylor is the only woman alive who comes close to Dolly's combination of songwriting, business power and global reach,' a veteran Nashville executive tells me before adding the cutting caveat: 'But Dolly made people forget their politics. Taylor brings politics into the room.'

Swift endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024 and has made no secret of her disdain for Donald Trump. So, Swift can kiss her Dolly crown goodbye.

Parton understood something almost no celebrity grasps anymore: Why opine on politics and risk alienating half your audience?

She spent decades refusing to become property of either tribe, declining the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times: twice from Trump, for personal and Covid-related reasons, and later from Joe Biden because she worried accepting it after rejecting Trump would look partisan.

As Parton put it: 'I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business… I'm not in politics, I'm an entertainer.'

Beyoncé belongs in the conversation, too.

Her country turn reinforced something Parton proved for decades: genres get more interesting when somebody opens the doors. Cowboy Carter made history, the supporting tour grossed over $400 million, making it the highest-grossing country roadshow ever, and the record itself won Best Country Album and Album of the Year at the 2025 Grammy Awards.

But Nashville power players don't see her ability to sustain a presence.

'Let's stop pretending Cowboy Carter was some flawless country masterpiece,' one Grammy award winner tells me. 'I thought the album was wildly overrated. And that Jolene cover? A complete misfire. Dolly's original is heartbreaking because it's vulnerable — Beyoncé turned it into a threat. That completely misses what makes the song so devastating.'

The source adds that Beyoncé's enormous talent isn't the issue:

'Beyoncé is one of the greatest performers alive. But the doesn't mean you're automatically great at country music. Nashville was terrified to say that out loud because nobody wanted to be accused of having some ulterior motive.'

There are a few other honorable mentions.

Reba McEntire is royalty: funny, warm and adored across generations.

'Reba has the affection, credibility and humor,' a country insider tells me. 'But Dolly escaped country. She belonged to people who didn't even know they liked country music.'

Grandmothers, gay men, church ladies, drag queens, conservatives, liberals, children and movie stars loved Parton. She achieved celebrity's rarest trick: broad affection without becoming bland.

Lainey Wilson may have the most interesting future because she has something increasingly rare: authenticity.

'Lainey has what Dolly had early,' a Nashville manager tells me. 'Within thirty seconds, you know exactly who she is. The problem is scale.'

Wilson, I'm told, is thought to lack the outsized personality to sit in Parton's throne.

'Ella Langley is having a moment, but moments come and go. I'm not convinced she has the staying power to still matter 30 years from now,' my Grammy-winning source says.

'Kacey Musgraves has the talent, the Grammys and the credibility, but she doesn't have Dolly's universal connection,' they added.

'Kacey is cool and critically adored, but Dolly was never just cool — she was loved. There's a huge difference. That kind of connection can't be manufactured, marketed or won at the Grammys.'

Then there is Miley Cyrus.

If Swift is Dolly's commercial heir, Cyrus may be her emotional one.

Parton was her godmother, and their relationship was real and lasting. Cyrus also has the crossover gene: country, rock, pop and blues all fit her.

'Miley inherited Dolly's fearlessness more than anyone,' a music-industry source tells me. 'Dolly controlled the joke before anyone could use it against her. Miley learned the same lesson: if people are going to talk, give them something worth talking about.'

Same survival instinct. Different bra.

In the end, however, true Music City insiders say all these divas may be spinning their wheels in the country mud.

'Everybody keeps asking who the next Dolly is,' a longtime entertainment executive tells me. 'There isn't one. The talent exists. The culture that created her doesn't.'

That is the real story. Broadcasting is dying – not just television or radio, but cultural broadcasting itself. We once watched the same shows, heard the same stations and knew the same stars. Now algorithms determine our viewing habits.

Your TikTok is different from mine. Your Spotify makes different suggestions. Your Netflix home screen looks like we live on different planets.

'A celebrity can have 20 million followers and still be invisible to half the country,' a top music booker tells me. 'We don't manufacture universal stars anymore because we don't have a universal culture anymore.'

Swift may be bigger commercially. Cyrus may be more wild. Wilson may become country's next great star. McEntire may remain its beloved grande dame.

But another Parton?

Honey, good luck.

Leave the crown exactly where she left it: empty, impossible to inherit and encrusted in rhinestones.

Rob Shuter's latest exclusives and insider reporting can be found at robshuter.substack.com

His best-selling novel is It Started With A Whisper
news.summary: 'Let's stop pretending Cowboy Carter was some flawless country masterpiece,' the Grammy award winner tells me.

news.title: Who Owns MapQuest? App Surges After Defying Trump on Lake America Change
news.text: MapQuest has found itself back in the national spotlight after publicly refusing to adopt President Donald Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario as "Lake America" on its maps. It's unclear who made the call not to update the map, but the head of the company that owns MapQuest isn't a fan of Trump's. Trump changed the name of Lake Ontario in an executive order last week as part of the escalating trade war between the United States and Canada. While some companies, including Google Maps, have updated their systems to reflect the name change, MapQuest has made it clear it won't change the name, just as it didn't change the name of the Gulf of Mexico when Trump changed it to the Gulf of America. In a social media message, the company said, "we're not changing it" in regard to the name change. MapQuest quickly got a boost, with downloads jumping more than 300 percent and the app becoming the number one downloaded app in Navigation. Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, told Newsweek, it was an "easy" decision to make. "People let us know we were making the right decision with their downloads back then, and they are downloading even more with Lake Ontario. Millions of people are realizing they have a choice in which mapping app they use," Berger said. The dispute over the lake's name has become the latest flashpoint in worsening U.S.-Canada relations following the collapse of trade talks between the two countries and the introduction of new tariffs. While federal agencies are expected to use the new designation, Canada has rejected the change and continues to recognize the body of water as Lake Ontario. “As the President said, the majority of the great lake’s volume sits in United States territory. Thanks to President Trump’s bold action, its name will now reflect its place in America and her heritage," Allison Schuster, a White House spokeswoman, told Newsweek via email. Who Owns MapQuest? MapQuest is owned by System1, a California-based advertising and consumer internet company. The mapping service has had several owners since it emerged as one of the internet's most recognizable brands during the 1990s. The CEO, Michael Blend, has made a number of political donations to Democrats, including to former Vice President Kamala Harris while she was running for president. It's unclear if Blend had any role in making the decision not to change the name. Blend gave Harris' campaign $2,000 in July 2024, about a week after Harris announced she'd be running for president. He previously donated to Harris' 2020 campaign, giving her $2,000 in 2019 and 2020. Blend also gave former President Joe Biden $2,800 when he ran for president in 2020, according to FEC records reviewed by Newsweek. Other political donations include: Originally launched in 1996, MapQuest became synonymous with online directions long before smartphone navigation apps existed. The service was later acquired by AOL and became part of Verizon's digital media holdings after Verizon purchased AOL. In 2019, System1 acquired MapQuest and has operated it since. Though it was largely eclipsed by Google Maps and Apple Maps in the smartphone era, the company's refusal to adopt Trump's renaming order unexpectedly thrust it back into public discourse. President Donald Trump called Apple about changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in the hopes of getting them to alter their maps, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Monday. MapQuest has embraced the attention. In addition to refusing to relabel the lake, the company launched an online tool allowing users to generate their own names for Lake Ontario. The move drew praise from some users, criticism from others, and considerable media coverage that helped revive interest in the decades-old platform. Newsweek reached out to Blend and MapQuest for comment via email but did not receive a response in time for publication. Did MapQuest Change the 'Gulf of America'? MapQuest also declined to adopt Trump's earlier renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. When Trump signed Executive Order 14172 in January 2025 directing federal agencies to use "Gulf of America," several major platforms eventually updated their maps for U.S. users. Google Maps implemented the change, and other services followed varying approaches. MapQuest, however, resisted the change. Instead of renaming the body of water on its maps, the company created a website feature that allowed users to assign their own names to the Gulf. The company has now used the same strategy in response to the Lake Ontario controversy, enabling visitors to generate custom labels for the lake. The consistency of MapQuest's stance has become part of the brand's messaging. After Trump announced the Lake Ontario change, the company joked by labeling the Great Lake "Lake Are We Doing This Again?" while reiterating that it had no plans to implement the federal designation. Why Did Donald Trump Change the Name of Lake Ontario? Trump announced the name change on August 27 after trade negotiations between the United States and Canada broke down and both countries imposed retaliatory tariffs. The president signed an executive order directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to update federal geographic databases and rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for official U.S. government use. Trump argued that the lake plays an important role in American commerce, trade, manufacturing, agriculture, energy production and military logistics. Speaking before signing the order, Trump said the change would take effect immediately. Federal agencies subsequently moved to update the Geographic Names Information System, the government's official repository for geographic names. The move was sharply criticized in Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the name Lake Ontario predates both Canada and the United States and originates from the Wendat language. He argued that the lake's historic name should remain unchanged despite the U.S. action. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told Newsweek renaming Lake Ontario is "deeply unserious" and "ridiculous." "In response to a trade war with Canada that Donald Trump started that’s going to make life more expensive for the American people, that’s ridiculous, they’re also deeply unserious, and we know this." Jeffries said. What is the Treaty of Canandaigua? The Treaty of Canandaigua is a 1794 agreement between the United States and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also known as the Iroquois Confederacy. Signed in Canandaigua, New York, during former President George Washington's administration, the treaty established peace between the United States and several Indigenous nations after the American Revolution. The agreement recognized land rights belonging to the Haudenosaunee nations and remains one of the most important treaties in Native American history. The federal government continues to acknowledge the treaty, and annual commemorations are held to recognize its significance. Indigenous leaders have argued that the lake's traditional name is rooted in Indigenous language and culture. Some critics of the renaming effort have pointed to long-standing Native American connections to the region when objecting to replacing the historic name with "Lake America." Did Google Maps Change Lake Ontario to Lake America? Google Maps began displaying "Lake America" for users located in the United States after the federal GNIS database was updated to reflect Trump's executive order. The company said the change is consistent with its long-standing practice of updating geographic names when official government sources make revisions. The display varies depending on location. According to Google, users in Canada continue to see "Lake Ontario." Users elsewhere in the world generally see both names displayed together, with Lake Ontario remaining the primary label. Google employed a similar approach following Trump's order renaming the Gulf of Mexico. The company previously said differing labels may appear depending on a user's geographic location and the naming conventions recognized by governments in those jurisdictions. What Was Lake Ontario Named After? Lake Ontario's name derives from the Wendat word "Ontari'io," which has been translated as meaning "beautiful lake," "great lake," or "lake of shining waters." Historical accounts indicate that forms of the name were recorded as early as the 17th century, centuries before the creation of modern Canada or the United States. The Province of Ontario later took its name from the lake rather than the other way around. Canadian officials have repeatedly pointed to the lake's Indigenous origins when defending its traditional name. Carney noted that the name is more than 400 years old and predates the founding documents of both countries. Representative Joe Courtney called changing the name an "insult" to tribal nations and an example of how "out of touch" and harmful it is to start "fights over issues that don't change anyone's lives, but also just alienate our friends." For supporters of the traditional designation, "Lake Ontario" represents centuries of geographic, cultural and Indigenous history. For Trump supporters, the new federal designation forms part of a broader campaign to emphasize American identity through changes to government place names. Whatever the outcome, the dispute has unexpectedly turned MapQuest, a company many assumed had faded into internet history, into one of the most talked-about names in tech. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Michael Blend, CEO of System1, which owns MapQuest, supported Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

news.title: What to know about the US primary election in Massachusetts
news.text:
Voters in the US state of Massachusetts head to the polls on Tuesday for a primary election featuring a closely watched United States Senate contest between Democratic incumbent Senator Ed Markey and US Representative Seth Moulton.

The race is the latest contest that pits the Democratic Party’s progressive and moderate wings against each other. But in a twist, Moulton, the challenger, is part of the moderate New Democrat Coalition, while Markey, the longtime progressive incumbent, is fighting to hold on to his seat.

Voters will also decide competitive Democratic primaries in the 6th and 8th Congressional Districts, as well as races for the state’s governor, state legislature, and district attorney.

What time do polls open and close in Massachusetts?

The Massachusetts primary is Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Polls open at 7am ET (11:00 GMT) and close at 8pm ET (midnight GMT).

What are the key races in the Massachusetts primary?

In the 6th District, voters will choose a Democratic nominee to succeed Moulton. The top contenders include former local election official Dan Koh, financial technology executive John Beccia, and Massachusetts State Representative Tram Nguyen.

Koh enters Tuesday as the leading fundraiser, with about $4.7m in contributions, and has endorsements from former US President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nguyen has raised about $895,000, while Beccia has boosted his campaign’s spending power with a $4m personal loan.

The winner will face Republican Micah Jones, who is unopposed for his party’s nomination.

In the 8th District, 13-term Democratic incumbent Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, faces a primary challenge from progressive attorney Patrick Roath, 39, who is endorsed by Leaders We Deserve, the political action committee (PAC) headed by gun-safety activist and political organiser David Hogg.

Roath has criticised the centrist voting record of Lynch, who broke with Democrats to vote against former US President Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act in March 2010, and who was Massachusetts’s only congressional member to vote for current US President Donald Trump’s Laken Riley Act, which requires federal law enforcement to detain and deport immigrants who have been charged with nonviolent crimes regardless of whether those charges ever result in a conviction.

The winner will face a midterm election against Republican Robert Burke, who runs uncontested and who lost his 2024 bid for Congress to Lynch.

In the gubernatorial race, the Democratic primary is effectively uncontested, with incumbent Governor Maura Healey running for the Democratic nomination, but with two Republican candidates vying for Healey’s seat. Brian Shortsleeve and Michael Roger Minogue, who are running in the GOP primary, are both military veterans with business backgrounds. The most notable difference between the two candidates is that Shortsleeve backs abortion rights, while Minogue does not. Both of them have supported Trump.

Who is running in the Massachusetts US Senate primary?

The biggest statewide contest is the Democratic US Senate primary between Markey and Moulton.

Markey is seeking a third full term, but faces a primary challenge from Moulton.

Markey, who turned 80 in July, entered the US Senate in 2013 after nearly 37 years in the US House of Representatives. He last faced a competitive primary in 2020, when he defeated then-Representative Joseph Kennedy III by 10 points. Moulton, a six-term congressman and Marine Corps veteran, briefly sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020.

Age has been a central theme of Moulton’s campaign. Markey, who turned 80 in July, is the oldest Senate Democrat running for re-election this year. Moulton, 47, has called for “generational change” in the Democratic Party, and argues that Markey is too old to represent a generation confronting challenges like artificial intelligence (AI).

Markey came under pressure during a recent debate, when he was asked whether he uses AI platforms such as ChatGPT or Claude in his work. Markey responded that he uses whatever is available through his iPhone or iPad, saying he did not know which companies his devices might be using.

Moulton seized on the exchange, arguing that leaders need to understand the technologies they will be responsible for regulating.

“Senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies,” Moulton said, calling Markey’s loose grasp of technology “potentially disqualifying”.

Markey defended his record on technology, arguing that familiarity with individual AI products is less important than establishing safeguards around the technology. He has pointed to legislation addressing AI’s effects on children, workers, civil rights and the environment.

Markey has won the endorsement of the High School Democrats of America and the College Democrats of America, as well as support from prominent progressives including US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Markey also has the support of US Senator Elizabeth Warren, a fellow Democrat from Massachusetts.

“Ed Markey is one of the strongest progressive voices in the United States Senate,” Sanders said in his endorsement of Markey. “He has been an ally in taking on the billionaires, Big Tech, Wall Street and private equity as they continue to try to take over every aspect of our lives and further corrupt our government.”

Recent polling has shown Markey with a sizable lead over Moulton.

A University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll conducted August 5-12 found Markey leading Moulton 60 percent to 32 percent, with 7 percent undecided.
news.summary: Competitive House races and a Senate showdown will put US Democrats’ progressive-moderate divide to the test.
